We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra's Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to 11923x with a median of 24.3x across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.
Optimization and Control.comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. v2: corrects three numerical values in Secs. III A, III E and V. Results unchanged

Optimization and Control.title: Non-singlets and the phase diagram of Matrix Quantum Mechanics
Optimization and Control.summary: The quantum mechanics of one $N\times N$ Hermitian matrix in the infinite $N$ limit is well known to define a two-dimensional string theory when the quartic coupling constant $g$ is tuned to a special negative value $g_*$. We study the thermodynamics of this Matrix Quantum Mechanics (MQM), treating the SU$(N)$ symmetry as a global symmetry. Crucially, the non-singlets, i.e. states in non-trivial representations of SU$(N)$, implement the effects of vortices on the discretized worldsheets. This random lattice model has the low-temperature $c=1$ and high-temperature $c=0$ phases, with the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition separating them. We map out the phase diagram in the coupling--temperature plane, which is separated by the critical stability curve $T_c(g)$ extending from $g_*< g <0$. We study this curve using the non-perturbative matrix bootstrap and low- and high-temperature perturbation theory, which explain the thermal instability. At low temperatures, thermally excited non-singlets backreact on the Fermi sea of matrix eigenvalues, causing it to spill over. At high temperatures, the theory is described by an effective matrix integral obtained by dimensional reduction on the thermal circle; the eigenvalue distribution of the zero mode becomes unstable at the critical coupling. We conjecture that the BKT transition occurs at a special point on the critical curve and estimate its position. Finally, we switch to the regular square lattice and study the MQM-inspired Villain model, where the link factor is the one-dimensional propagator on a circle. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we map out the BKT transition in this model.

Optimization and Control.title: Multiplicative vs. Additive State Coupling in Learned Optimizer Schedules
Optimization and Control.summary: We learn schedules for a continuous penalty relaxation of MAX-CUT by backpropagating through an unrolled classical solver. A state-blind schedule generalizes to instances substantially larger than those used for training. A state-adaptive bilinear schedule also generalizes out of distribution, outperforming its untrained baseline across 15 seeds ($t=4.1$). By contrast, an additive ablation with identical inputs and output heads is statistically indistinguishable from the bilinear model in distribution but performs worse than its own baseline out of distribution ($t=-11.7$). This separation appears without regularization and persists across a $30$ round weight-decay sweep: the bilinear advantage remains significant at every tested value, whereas the additive model never recovers. The results in this setting isolate how solver state enters the schedule, rather than state adaptivity alone, as the architectural distinction associated with out-of-distribution transfer.

Optimization and Control.title: A path-following framework on fiber bundle for variational inequalities
Optimization and Control.summary: Developing general-purpose algorithms with global asymptotic convergence guarantees for variational inequalities (VIs) remains a longstanding challenge. This paper proposes a path-following framework for finite-dimensional VIs with arbitrary continuous mappings and polytope domains. The approach first transforms a general VI into a smooth VI on a simplex. Its key innovation is to formulate the resulting problem on a fiber bundle, called the fixed-point bundle, whose geometric structure enables the systematic integration of initialization, path-following, and singularity avoidance. Without imposing monotonicity or similar assumptions, the framework guarantees global linear convergence for nonsingular solutions and global linear convergence up to any prescribed precision for singular solutions. In numerical experiments, the algorithm attained a precision of $10^{-5}$ on all 6400 randomly generated instances, with dimensions up to 1024. Code and data are available at https://github.com/shb20tsinghua/FiberBundle_VI.
Optimization and Control.comment: 29 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, code and data are available at https://github.com/shb20tsinghua/FiberBundle_VI

Optimization and Control.title: The fixed-point bundle method over product-of-simplex domains arising from game equilibria
Optimization and Control.summary: Developing general-purpose algorithms with global asymptotic convergence guarantees for Nash equilibria of general-sum games remains a longstanding challenge. This paper extends the fixed-point bundle framework for finite-dimensional variational inequalities (VIs) from simplex domains to product-of-simplex domains, enabling its direct application to Nash equilibrium computation. The resulting fixed-point bundle exhibits a composite fiber bundle structure. The key innovation is to construct an equivalent VI on a simplex and establish the equivalence between the two fixed-point bundle frameworks via a fiber bundle isomorphism. Exploiting this geometric equivalence, we show that the path-following algorithm for VIs on product-of-simplex domains inherits the global linear convergence guarantees of the simplex-domain framework. In numerical experiments, the algorithm attained a precision of $10^{-5}$ on all 5600 randomly generated game instances, with dimension ranging from 2-player 128-action to 128-player 2-action. Code and data are available at https://github.com/shb20tsinghua/FiberBundle_VI.
Optimization and Control.comment: 26 pages, 1 table, code and data are available at https://github.com/shb20tsinghua/FiberBundle_VI

Optimization and Control.title: G-ORACLE: A Fast Geometric Method To Explore All Near-Optimal Designs for Energy Systems
Optimization and Control.summary:
Modeling to Generate Alternatives (MGA) methods explore the near-optimal solutions of energy system optimization models (ESOMs), i.e., alternative planning pathways whose cost lies within a small predefined slack of the optimum but which can differ substantially in technology composition, regional distribution, and environmental impacts. Among MGA methods, ORACLE uniquely guarantees convergence to the near-optimal set within a targeted tolerance by iteratively refining inner and outer polytope approximations. At each iteration, given a trial point, it solves a problem as hard as the ESOM to find the nearest near-optimal solution to it. However, the trial point is obtained by solving a bilevel problem whose solution time grows rapidly with the number of iterations and eventually dominates the computational cost of the method.
  To eliminate this bottleneck, we present G-ORACLE, which exploits the fact that an optimal solution of the bilevel problem is always attained at a vertex of the outer approximation. G-ORACLE therefore replaces the bilevel problem with incremental vertex enumeration by the double description method and one convex projection per vertex, while retaining the convergence guarantee of ORACLE. A supporting-hyperplane check further avoids unnecessary recomputation of these projections as the inner approximation grows.
  We evaluate G-ORACLE on an electricity-only PyPSA-Eur model, exploring the near-optimal space of the installed capacities of six generation and two storage technologies. While ORACLE's bilevel problem exceeds 20 minutes at iteration 64, G-ORACLE performs the trial-point search in at most 14 seconds throughout 240 iterations, leaving the ESOM solves as the only significant computational cost.

Optimization and Control.title: Stochastic Inverse Problem: stability, regularization and Wasserstein gradient flow
Optimization and Control.summary: Inverse problems in physical or biological sciences often involve recovering an unknown parameter that is random. The sought-after quantity is a probability distribution of the unknown parameter, that produces data that aligns with measurements. Consequently, these problems are naturally framed as stochastic inverse problems. In this paper, we explore three aspects of this problem: direct inversion, variational formulation with regularization, and optimization via gradient flows, drawing parallels with deterministic inverse problems. A key difference from the deterministic case is the space in which we operate. Here, we work within a probability space rather than Euclidean or Sobolev spaces, making tools from measure transport theory necessary for the study. Our findings reveal that the choice of metric---both in the design of the loss function and in the optimization process---significantly impacts the stability and properties of the optimizer.

Optimization and Control.title: A Proximal Gradient Method for Nonconvex Nonsmooth Optimization with Applications
Optimization and Control.summary: We study a proximal-gradient method for the sum of a convex smooth function $g$ and a possibly nonconvex, nonsmooth, strongly quasar-convex regularizer. The gradient step is weighted by the quasar-convexity parameter, so, for step sizes in the descent range, the iteration decreases a weighted objective, while the unweighted sum serves for comparison. We establish a geometric envelope around every global minimizer of the unweighted objective, with an explicit radius independent of the step size; a common minimizer yields global linear convergence. We also prove that every critical point $u$ of the weighted objective lies within an explicit multiple of $\|\nabla g(u)\|$ from every global minimizer of the unweighted objective. Together with an optimized composite comparison, this yields asymptotic distance bounds. An example shows that the two objectives can have different critical points. For power-regularized least squares with powers between zero and one, descent provides a confinement ball for the sharp local modulus, and support identification combined with a KL argument yields whole-sequence convergence.

Optimization and Control.title: Superlinear Convergence of Cyclic Gradient Methods with Historical Ritz Step Sizes
Optimization and Control.summary: Simplified spectral models predict dimension-dependent superlinear convergence for gradient methods, but the corresponding behavior of actual iterations remains only partially understood. Historical methods introduce an additional difficulty: the gradients defining the step sizes differ from those receiving them. We study this offset for cyclic reuse of historical Ritz step sizes on strictly convex quadratics. Within the existing limited memory steepest descent with retards (LMSDR) family, a rolling cyclic Ritz (RCR) rule reuses $m$ historical Ritz values $\ell$ times per cycle, ending with a complete sweep. At $q=m+1$ active distinct eigenvalues, an exact delayed recurrence gives almost-everywhere doubly exponential convergence with an explicit rate and exceptional weights. Nonempty open basins also exist for $m+1<q\le2m$ and $\ell\ge4$. Rebuilding the history from each cycle-start gradient costs $m$ additional updates and gives sampled cyclic Ritz reuse (SCR) a cycle-end map determined by the current weights. Under uniform sampling bounds, SCR converges doubly exponentially almost everywhere when $(2\ell-1)^m>\binom{q-1}{m}$. Increasing $\ell$ admits larger $q$ for fixed $m$. The guarantee extends to history-dependent choices from finite sampling menus under a bound on the number of admissible sampling sequences. Geometrically spaced decisions retain the SCR condition and rate range. Every update is counted, including sampling; a numerical illustration compares finite-tolerance update counts.

Optimization and Control.title: Necessary and Sufficient Criteria for Global PID Regulation of Nonlinear Uncertain System
Optimization and Control.summary: Although classical PID control is widely used in engineering practice, identifying all PID gains that guarantee global regulation of nonlinear uncertain dynamics remains challenging. For a class of second-order nonaffine systems under one-sided derivative bounds, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for global PID regulation: a fixed PID controller globally regulates the entire infinite-dimensional uncertainty class if and only if it regulates a single boundary linear system. Applying the Routh--Hurwitz criterion to this boundary linear system yields the exact admissible PID gain region. To establish this equivalence, we prove a structured Markus--Yamabe theorem for third-order integrator chains under uniform derivative-ratio conditions. Its proof combines a two-dimensional storage function constructed via viscosity solutions of a Hamilton--Jacobi equation with a scalar comparison argument. We further show that the same PID gain region remains exact for multidimensional affine systems under symmetry assumptions on the state partial Jacobians and the input matrix.

Optimization and Control.title: Regret-Based Scenario-Tree Construction for Multistage Stochastic Programs with Deterministic Constraints
Optimization and Control.summary:
Scenario trees are widely used to discretize multistage stochastic programs into forms that are tractable for numerical optimization. Yet, traditional scenario-tree construction methods are typically based on statistical similarity between the original uncertainty process and its discretization, and may fail to preserve the aspects of the uncertainty that matter most for decision-making.
  This paper shows that, under a fixed probability measure and deterministic feasibility constraints, the gap between the optimal value of the original multistage stochastic program and that of its scenario-tree approximation decomposes exactly into a sum of nodewise regret terms, each measuring the optimality loss at a particular node. This decomposition provides a clear target for scenario-tree construction: minimizing total regret across the tree. Motivated by this result, we propose a practical two-phase construction method for repeated stochastic optimization. In an offline phase, computationally inexpensive surrogates for decision regret are learned from data, and in the online phase, these surrogates guide scenario-tree construction. The resulting framework retains the structured optimization and constraint-handling capabilities of multistage stochastic programming while exploiting learned information about the uncertainty to make more effective use of a limited scenario-tree budget.
  Numerical experiments on multistage stochastic storage and production-planning problems show that, for a fixed tree size, the proposed method constructs higher-quality scenario trees and achieves better closed-loop performance than traditional scenario-tree construction methods.
Optimization and Control.comment: Submitted to the European Journal of Operational Research

Optimization and Control.title: Safe Leader-Follower Density Control via Higher-Order Mean-Field Control Barrier Functions
Optimization and Control.summary: Mean-field control barrier functions (MF-CBFs) enforce safety of large-scale multi-agent systems at the level of densities, but existing formulations require the control to act directly on the population to be kept safe. We consider populations that are not directly actuated and are influenced only through other, controlled populations, possibly in the presence of diffusion. We show that if the constrained population lies at directed graph distance d from the actuated one, then, under a nondegeneracy condition, the safety functional has relative degree d+1 and the control enters its (d+1)-th time derivative affinely. Higher-order safety constraints can therefore still be enforced through a convex quadratic program. We apply the framework to leader-follower density control among dangerous regions, where the follower safety functional has relative degree two and the leader safety functional has relative degree one. We characterize exactly when the two constraints are jointly infeasible and bound the tracking errors induced by the safety correction. Simulations in cluttered environments show that the proposed filter preserves follower safety, whereas enforcing leader safety alone does not.

Optimization and Control.title: Pauli-Sparse regularised Counterdiabatic Shortcuts for Linear-Ramp QAOA
Optimization and Control.summary:
Combinatorial optimization is a leading target for quantum algorithms, but finite-depth QAOA can suffer from strong diabatic errors when the interpolation Hamiltonian has small, or exponentially small, spectral gaps. We propose a Pauli-sparse counterdiabatic extension of linear-ramp QAOA based on the regularised adiabatic gauge potential \[
  \bigl(\mathcal L_H^2+ηI\bigr)A_λ^{(η)}
  =
  -\mathrm{i}\mathcal L_H(\partial_λH),
  \qquad
  \mathcal L_H(X)=[H,X]. \] Instead of computing a dense AGP, we solve this equation approximately by an inexact conjugate-gradient method in Pauli coordinates, truncating the Pauli expansion during the iteration to obtain a gate-budget-aware set of implementable rotations. The selected support is then improved by a Galerkin refit and certified by an a posteriori residual bound. The regularization parameter \(η\) acts as an energy-resolution scale: it suppresses transitions below \(\sqrtη\) while retaining larger-gap transitions. Thus, the method can avoid resolving exponentially small splittings inside a low-energy solution manifold while reducing leakage away from it. Numerical experiments on Ferromagnetic Chain (FC) and perturbed FC--MaxCut/MarketSplit instances show that the resulting LR-CD-QAOA ansatz improves approximation ratios over the uncorrected linear ramp, especially in regimes where LR-QAOA remains far from the optimum. Overall, the proposed regularized LR-CD-QAOA framework substantially broadens the practical applicability of QAOA to QUBO optimization by improving its robustness across heterogeneous problem landscapes, including instances with near-degenerate low-energy structures and small spectral gaps.

Optimization and Control.title: The iterates of FISTA converge even under inexact computations and stochastic gradients
Optimization and Control.summary: Very recently, the papers "Point Convergence of Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Method: An AI-Assisted Proof" by Jang and Ryu, and "The Iterates of Nesterov's Accelerated Algorithm Converge in the Critical Regimes" by Bot, Fadili, and Nguyen have simultaneously resolved a long-standing open problem concerning Nesterov's accelerated gradient method. These works show that the iterates of the algorithm (known in its composite form as FISTA) indeed converge to an optimal solution. In this work, we extend these results and prove that, in infinite dimensional Hilbert spaces, the iterates of such an algorithm still converge (in the weak sense) even when the proximity operator and the gradient are computed inexactly, with the latter possibly stochastic. Our framework covers both absolute and relative errors in proximal computations. In the stochastic setting, it allows for uniformly bounded variance as well as proximal counterparts of strong growth conditions, under which iterate convergence can be established while retaining accelerated objective-value rates.

Optimization and Control.title: An Optimal Projection Framework for Structure-Preserving Model Reduction of Linear Systems
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper presents a model order reduction framework for linear systems where the $\mathcal{H}_2$ optimization is combined with the Petrov-Galerkin projection to preserve a wide range of system properties, including stability, bounded realness, sector boundedness, and dissipativity. The model reduction problem is formulated as a nonconvex optimization problem on a generalized Stiefel manifold, aiming to minimize the $\mathcal{H}_2$ norm of the pproximation error between the full-order and reduced-order models. An explicit expression for the Euclidean gradient of the objective function is derived, and a Riemannian gradient procedure with an efficient generalized Cayley update is applied to seek a (locally) optimal projection, followed by a theoretical analysis of the algorithm. Finally, the performance of the proposed method is demonstrated by a numerical example.
Optimization and Control.comment: accepted by IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control

Optimization and Control.title: Contextual Decision Making: Predictive or Generative
Optimization and Control.summary: Contextual decision making uses observed covariates to guide decisions under uncertainty. Two natural approaches are predict-then-optimize (PtO), which learns the conditional expected objective, and generate-then-optimize (GtO), which learns conditional uncertainty and optimizes using generated scenarios. We study when each approach is preferable by examining how the choice of learning target affects statistical accuracy and optimization tractability. Although PtO learns a narrower target, our regret bounds show how differences in smoothness can offset GtO's additional dimensional burden. Exploiting smoothness also raises an optimization tradeoff: within the class of nonnegative-weight PtO methods studied, a lower bound limits the gains from additional smoothness, while more flexible methods may introduce signed weights and lose the guarantee of preserving convexity. GtO preserves scenario-wise convexity, but requires learning a richer object and generating scenarios for optimization. Synthetic experiments and a real case study illustrate how these tradeoffs vary with data availability and problem structure. Together with the scope for reusing a model across tasks, our findings provide practical guidance for choosing between the approaches without identifying a universal winner.

Optimization and Control.title: Momentum in large-batch training: Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, Nesterov improves data efficiency
Optimization and Control.summary: We study when and how momentum improves large-batch training in the one-pass regime, using power-law kernel regression as a tractable setting. We first characterize risk stability through the \emph{critical learning rate}, defined as the largest learning rate for stable training, and obtain $η_{\mathrm{SGD}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim 1$, $η_{\mathrm{Polyak}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim \min\{1,B(1-β)\}$, and $η_{\mathrm{Nesterov}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim \min\{1,B^q(1-β)\}$, where $B$ is the batch size, $β$ is the momentum factor, and $q>1$ is the capacity exponent. Within this admissible region, we derive scaling laws for the full risk dynamics, capturing the progression from an early transient, through power-law decay, to a noise floor. We then minimize the final-step risk over the admissible learning rates and momentum factors under a fixed data budget, yielding a three-regime batch-size phase diagram that reveals how the role of momentum changes with batch size. Notably, Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, the largest batch size preserving the best small-batch data-scaling exponent, thereby enabling greater parallelism without sacrificing data efficiency. In contrast, Nesterov achieves better data efficiency in the large-batch regime because its look-ahead mechanism suppresses noise accumulation. Numerical experiments validate the predicted stability boundaries, risk dynamics, and batch-size phase diagram.

Optimization and Control.title: Who pays for urban environment management? The role of the third-party service provider
Optimization and Control.summary: The dominant contemporary paradigm of direct state-led urban environmental regulation entails significant risks, including high administrative burden, frequent conflicts with polluting entities, and economic vulnerabilities for those sources. To address these deficiencies, this paper integrates third-party service provider (TPSP) into China's existing management framework as a beneficial extension beyond conventional government intervention. Utilizing an evolutionary game approach, we compare two distinct institutional settings, a non-integration management mode and an integration management mode, and scrutinize the evolutionary dynamics across both two- and three-dimensional systems. To enhance system robustness, we embed a strategic behavior-based dynamic punishment mechanism that effectively eliminates the perturbing effects of varied penalty rules, thereby steering all stakeholders toward an ideal stable state. This comparative institutional analysis isolates the marginal contribution of third-party intermediation, specifies when outsourcing environmental services outperforms direct government enforcement, and reframes evolutionary game theory as a design device for institutional self-correction. Furthermore, a predefined variable importance analysis is conducted to highlight critical factors warranting attention in practical policy implementation. Extensive simulation experiments, carried out under diverse system-level and parameter-level conditions, validate the theoretical properties of our model. The findings offer concrete managerial insights to inform the formulation of more effective urban environmental supervision regulations.

Optimization and Control.title: Exact Reachability under Vertex- and Area-Centroid Control
Optimization and Control.summary:
A vertex-centroid move slides one vertex of a polygon along the line through it and the centroid of all vertices; Problem 60 of The Open Problems Project asks whether such moves can make every polygon regular. We prove that two simple labeled $n$-gons, with straight angles allowed, are joined through simple polygons by finitely many positive moves exactly when they have the same orientation; a nonconstant move is positive if the vertex remains on the same side of the centroid of the other vertices. The same holds for flows toward or away from the instantaneous area centroid. Inward-only or outward-only moves reach every target of the same orientation up to translation and positive scaling.
  The common mechanism is a first-order criterion: a symmetric definite center response makes the one-vertex fields of a smooth affine-equivariant center bracket generating. The response is a weighted covariance for point barycenters and $(d+2)$ times the volume covariance for polyhedral centroids. Once translation and scale are factored out, the fields sum to zero, giving exact one-sided control. We resolve Problem 60 under both conventions for a vertex at the centroid. For the vertex-centroid system on $n$ affinely spanning points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we classify positive-move reachability and prove a local $3dn$-move bound.

Optimization and Control.title: Dual companions and improved regularity of Lagrange multipliers in optimal control
Optimization and Control.summary: We investigate optimal control problems whose state equation takes the form $\mathcal{A}x-\mathcal{B}u=b$, where $\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{P}'$ is an isomorphism from a Banach state space $\mathcal{X}$ onto the dual of a reflexive Banach space $\mathcal{P}$. The adjoint equation involves the Banach space adjoint $\mathcal{A}':\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{X}'$, so that, in general, state and multiplier are of different regularity. For particular classes of partial differential equations, the typically weaker regularity of the multiplier is improved a posteriori by bootstrapping. In this work, we provide an abstract foundation for this methodology on the operator level. More precisely, we show that whenever the state cost extends to a differentiable function on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ in which $\mathcal{X}$ is densely embedded, as for $L^2$-tracking costs on Sobolev-type state spaces, the multiplier automatically lies in a subspace of $\mathcal{P}$, the dual companion, on which $\mathcal{A}'$ restricts to an isomorphism onto $\mathcal{H}'$. This yields an optimality system with balanced regularity, where state and multiplier solve equations of the same type. In applications, the dual companion can be identified by integration by parts in time or space. We illustrate the framework by linear elliptic and parabolic equations, Cauchy problems governed by general $C_0$-semigroups, and a wave equation with accumulated-state observation.

Optimization and Control.title: On the $q$-integrability of $p$-Wasserstein barycenters
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the $L^q$-regularity of the density of barycenters of $N$ probability measures on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to the $p$-Wasserstein metric ($1<p<\infty$). According to a previous result by the first author and collaborators, if one marginal is absolutely continuous, so is the $W_p$-barycenter. The next natural question is whether the $L^q$- regularity on the marginals is also preserved for any $q > 1$, as in the classical case ($p=2$) of Agueh--Carlier, or for $W_p$-geodesics ($N=2$). Here we prove that this is the case if one marginal belongs to $L^q$ and the supports of all the marginals satisfy suitable geometric assumptions. However, we show that, as soon as $N>2$, it is possible to find examples of $W_p$-barycenters which are not $q$-integrable, even if one marginal is compactly supported and bounded, thus highlighting the role played by the geometry of the supports. Furthermore, we provide a general estimate of the $L^q$-norm, including a detailed study of the sources of singularities, and a characterization of the $W_p$-barycenters à la Agueh--Carlier in terms of the associated Kantorovich potentials. Finally, we explicitly compute the $W_p$-barycenters of measures obtained as push-forward of special affine transformations. In this case, regularity holds without any additional requirement on the supports.

Optimization and Control.title: L0-Norm-Based CycleGAN for Unpaired Brain CT-to-MR Synthesis
Optimization and Control.summary: Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance (MR) imaging provide complementary information for the brain, but acquiring both modalities is not always possible. The cycle-consistent adversarial network (CycleGAN) enables unpaired CT-to-MR synthesis, but because the standard L1-norm cycle?consistency penalty grows linearly with the residual magnitude, the network tends to focus on large residuals. This paper introduces an L0-norm-based cycle?consistency term, in which the L0-norm is approximated by a smooth and bounded function. This approximation not only increases sensitivity to small residuals but also effectively suppresses the influence of large residuals. The proposed model and an otherwise identical L1-norm baseline were trained on 102 images and evaluated on 9 test images. The proposed model achieves a lower mean squared error (0.02746 versus 0.03464, a 20.7% reduction), a higher mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (15.80 versus 14.77 dB), and a higher mean structural similarity index (0.5689 versus 0.5407). It also has a lower maximum MSE and higher minimum PSNR and SSIM than the baseline. These results indicate that modifying the cycle-consistency penalty can improve reconstruction accuracy on this dataset.

Optimization and Control.title: Adaptive Schauder Stochastic Mirror Descent in Banach Spaces
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper, we introduce an adaptive regularization strategy for stochastic mirror descent (SMD) to solve a class of risk functional minimization problems in infinite-dimensional Banach spaces. Using a Schauder basis, we construct nested finite-dimensional subspaces whose dimensions adapt to the sample size $n$ and balance approximation and optimization errors. We restrict each SMD subproblem to the corresponding subspace and project the stochastic gradient onto its dual space. This yields closed form solutions and coordinate-wise coefficient updates with low computational and storage complexity. For risk minimization in $\mathcal{L}^p$ spaces with $1<p<\infty$, we construct Bregman distances adapted to the underlying Banach space geometry using $\max\{2,p\}$-convex functionals induced by uniform convexity. At the $\mathcal{L}^1$ endpoint, we instead construct a locally strongly convex functional based on the entropy function. By developing a new analytical framework, we establish a convergence rate of $\mathcal O\left(n^{-\min\{\frac12,\frac1p\}}\right)$, up to logarithmic factors. In the misspecified setting, we prove convergence of the risk to its minimum under weaker regularity assumptions and derive explicit polynomial rates when the regularity exceeds a specified threshold. Finally, we apply the method to statistical inverse problems and illustrate its empirical performance through numerical experiments in both settings.

Optimization and Control.title: Sharpness-aware Orthogonalized Momentum Algorithms
Optimization and Control.summary: Adversarial sharpness penalty per iteration of a base optimizer, known as sharpness-aware minimization (SAM), is an accepted technique to improve generalization in deep learning. Recently, Muon has emerged as a dominant optimization algorithm for training large language models (LLMs). It achieves lower sample complexity for heavy-tailed gradient updates - a phenomenon common in LLM training. However, sharpness penalties with Muon updates are yet largely unexplored in the literature. Moreover, the behavior of SAM under heavy-tailed noise is unknown both theoretically and empirically. A potential reason for this gap is the additional cost of extra gradient computation per iteration for penalty perturbations in SAM, which becomes prohibitive for LLMs. This paper introduces Sharpness-aware Orthogonalized Momentum Algorithm (SOMA) to combine a computationally efficient and theoretically grounded perturbation scheme with the Muon algorithm. The key idea is to use stale (purely) stochastic gradient noise for adversarial perturbations. Theoretically, we show that SOMA's sample complexity is invariant to the perturbation direction. We provide explorations and insights into SOMA's robustness to heavy-tailed gradient noise. We extensively explore SOMA's efficacy in (a) mitigating quality degradation due to post-training quantization, and (b) catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning of LLMs.

Optimization and Control.title: On the closure under barycenters of location-scatter families with a normalized generator
Optimization and Control.summary: We provide an example of a normalized absolutely continuous probability whose location-scatter family (LSF) does not contain all the 2-Wassertein geodesics passing through its elements. In particular, we find a counterexample for Corollary 4.5 in [2]. Finally, we prove that LSFs with a (possibly singular) radially symmetric generator are closed under 2-Wasserstein barycenters.

Optimization and Control.title: Generalized Wasserstein Flow Matching: Nested Couplings for Point Cloud Generation
Optimization and Control.summary: We formulate flow matching on probability measures over probability measures. Directly from the Wasserstein-on-Wasserstein (WoW) continuity equation, we show that admissible nested outer and inner couplings induce a valid metameasure flow and non-local velocity field. Validity requires neither optimal plans nor a smooth manifold. Practically, this opens up the design space of multisample flow matching: exact Wasserstein plans are distinguished by energy and straightness, while sliced and lazy linear plans yield scalable alternatives. Point-cloud experiments, including controlled Bures-Wasserstein and Euclidean minibatch baselines, demonstrate the resulting geometry-cost trade-off.
Optimization and Control.comment: Keywords: flow matching, Wasserstein over Wasserstein, hierarchical optimal transport, multisample flow matching, minibatch optimal transport, sliced Wasserstein, Bures-Wasserstein, point cloud generation, generative models for distributions, measure-valued data, Wasserstein gradient flow, rectified flow, straight flows

Optimization and Control.title: Generalized fluctuation bounds for stochastic algorithms in the presence of compactness
Optimization and Control.summary: We provide a convergence result for sequences of random variables taking values in a metric space that satisfy a stochastic quasi-Fejér monotonicity condition, in the context of a (local) compactness assumption. Our result is quantitative in that we derive an explicit and effective construction which, in terms of only a few moduli representing quantitative witnesses to key properties of the sequence of random variables and the underlying metric space involved, provides a metastable rate of pointwise convergence, a type of generalized fluctuation bound. That quantitative result in particular relies on the development of a finitary theory of martingales, culminating in a fully finitary Robbins-Siegmund theorem. We outline how this result particularises to the circumstances of the seminal work of Combettes and Pesquet on stochastic quasi-Fejér monotone sequences in separable Hilbert spaces, and we provide an initial application by illustrating how these results can be used to provide a metastable rate of pointwise convergence for a stochastic Krasnoselskii-Mann scheme solving a stochastic common fixed point problem for nonexpansive maps over proper Hadamard spaces. This work is set in the context of recent applications of the logic-based methodology of proof mining to probability theory, and represents its most sophisticated case study to date.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Limits of Stochastic Push-Pull over Time-Varying Digraphs
Optimization and Control.summary: Stochastic Push-Pull achieves linear speedup with respect to the network size $n$ on static strongly connected digraphs, but whether this speedup persists on time-varying networks remains unclear. In this work, we construct a quadratic decentralized problem on period-two networks showing that stochastic Push-Pull may fail to attain linear speedup over time-varying digraphs. For $p$-periodic networks, we identify an effective node count $n_{\mathrm{eff}}\le n$ that governs the leading stochastic term. Specifically, for smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish convergence upper bounds and matching lower bounds for stochastic Push-Pull with constant stepsizes, both exhibiting the leading-order dependence $Θ(1/\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{eff}} T})$. When $p=1$, the identity $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=n$ recovers the usual linear speedup for static digraphs. However, periodic networks can have $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=o(n)$, demonstrating the loss of linear speedup under temporal variation. Numerical experiments illustrate effective-count scaling and the separation between static and periodic networks, consistent with our theoretical findings.

Optimization and Control.title: MIACE and Monotone Tracking: Exact Tuning for First-Order Plants and Positive Cascades with Pure Delay
Optimization and Control.summary: The Module of Integral Absolute Complex Error (MIACE) was created by me 23 years ago. It gave very nice behaviour to the transient response of the controlled systems I tested. It combines absolute tracking-error and equilibrium-centered command areas. For a stable unit-gain plant with known pure delay, an exact identity separates squared MIACE excess into a negative-area penalty and a weighted area imbalance. The resulting lower bound depends on the plant's first low-frequency moment and the delay. Every attaining response of a positive cascade is monotone, independently of controller structure. For a first-order plant, output variation and peak overshoot also admit quantitative bounds. Exact conditions identify the unique positive PI controller attaining the delayed bound; filtered PID extends attainment beyond this PI range. For cascades of arbitrary order, Hermite interpolation and a finite-support delay remainder construct proper rational controllers of the same order, with internal exponential stability proved by positive convolution representations. An exponential-moment characterization then closes the attainment question when internal delay blocks are allowed: an ordinary command attains the bound if and only if $α>μ+δ-1$. An explicit internal-model controller realizes every feasible weight and delay. A sharp amplitude-cap condition determines the least command peak among all attaining responses and the complete capped sign-preserving area front. A small-gain estimate supplies an explicit MIACE deviation bound under delay error. A storage balance also extends the exact MIACE identity and monotone attainment to a nonlinear first-order class without delay. Independent physical integrations retain delays exactly; quadratic comparisons provide complementary benchmarks.

Optimization and Control.title: Source reconstruction algorithms for coupled parabolic systems from internal measurements of one scalar state
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper is devoted to the study of source reconstruction algorithms for coupled systems of heat equations, with either constant or spatially dependent coupling terms, where internal measurements are available from a reduced number of observed states. Two classes of systems are considered. The first comprises parabolic equations with constant zero-order coupling terms (through a matrix potential term or via the diffusion matrix). The second type considers parabolic equations coupled by a matrix potential that depends on spatial variables, which leads to the analysis of a non-self-adjoint operator. In all configurations, the source is assumed to be of separate variables, the temporal part is a known scalar function, and the spatial dependence is an unknown vector field. Several numerical examples using the finite element method in 1D and 2D are presented to show the reconstruction of space-dependent sources.

Optimization and Control.title: A Robust Control Architecture for Multirate Systems and their Interconnections
Optimization and Control.summary: We introduce a framework for analyzing and designing linear multirate control systems and their interconnections through the lens of robust control. The proposed approach models multirate systems as impulsive systems with multiple independent jump maps and corresponding jump-time sequences. We tackle analysis and design problems with stability, dissipativity, and robustness objectives, relying on a multi-clock-dependent Lyapunov function parameterization. Further, we develop a compositional approach for analyzing interconnections of multirate systems based on individual dissipativity properties. The theoretical conditions can be verified via linear matrix inequalities and they require weak assumptions on the sampling rates, allowing for asynchronous and time-varying sampling rates with or without separated time scales. The practicality of the framework is demonstrated with numerical examples.

Optimization and Control.title: A Counterexample to the Optimality Conjecture in Convex Quantum Channel Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper presents a counterexample to the optimality conjecture for the trace distance based optimal state transformation problem proposed by Coutts et al. [Quantum 5, 448 (2021)]. The conjecture posits that for the trace distance based optimal state transformation problem, applying the sign function to the error matrix uniquely determines a dual certificate for every optimal solution. By constructing a counterexample in 2-dimensional Hilbert spaces, we disprove this conjecture.

Optimization and Control.title: Mapping Academic Sports Analytics: A Content Analysis of JQAS and JSA
Optimization and Control.summary: Sports analytics has expanded rapidly in professional sports and mainstream culture, yet defining its academic core remains a challenge. In this paper, we provide an empirical map of the academic sports analytics landscape based on a systematic content analysis of approximately 700 papers published in two leading dedicated journals, the Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports (JQAS) and the Journal of Sports Analytics (JSA), between the years 2005 and 2024. We classify each paper by sport discipline, mathematical method, and core research area, identify recurring themes, and examine macro trends. We find game tactics, player evaluation, team ranking, result forecasting, and tournament design to be the most studied research areas in sports analytics. We highlight selected papers in each area, illustrating the wide range of mathematical methods used and sports disciplines analyzed. Our work offers a comprehensive overview of the questions, methods, and disciplines that characterize the field, serving as a foundational reference for practitioners and researchers in sports analytics.

Optimization and Control.title: Individual Minima-Informed Multi-Objective Model Predictive Control for Fixed Point Stabilization
Optimization and Control.summary: In multi-objective model predictive control (MOMPC), a single Pareto-optimal solution has to be selected at each sampling instant by an automated a priori decision-making (DM) mechanism, since real-time constraints do not permit a human decision-maker to be involved. This paper considers MOMPC for fixed point stabilization, where the DM translates a high-level preference into the solution to be implemented, while closed-loop stability has to be preserved. To this end, an approach called individual minima-informed DM is introduced. These methods leverage the individual minima, which are characteristic Pareto-optimal points, to facilitate the translation of a high-level preference to a point on the Pareto front. They can be implemented through two sequential optimizations, regardless of the number of objectives, thereby facilitating a real-time implementation of MOMPC. Two novel methods are proposed and compared with four established ones. These methods are embedded into a stabilizing MOMPC scheme that builds on a quasi-infinite horizon framework from the literature. Closed-loop stability is proven under a descent condition that is less restrictive than the one in the original framework and retains the largest DM space among all descent conditions that prevent any objective from increasing. The required terminal ingredients can be constructed with a practical procedure. In a numerical case study, the resulting scheme stabilizes the fixed point and illustrates the potential benefit of adapting the preference online.

Optimization and Control.title: A stochastic mirror descent algorithm for mean-field control problems
Optimization and Control.summary: We develop a stochastic mirror descent method for continuous-time McKean-Vlasov control with measure-valued controls and general Bregman regularisation. The dependence on the state law leads to a coupled Wasserstein-Bregman stability problem and to a McKean-Vlasov adjoint equation, which have no counterpart in classical stochastic control. We establish a first-order representation of the cost and prove its relative smoothness in two regimes: nonlinear dynamics with bounded cost derivatives, and affine state-law dynamics with linearly growing cost derivatives, the latter covering linear-quadratic (LQ) and more general nonquadratic models. Our regularity conditions in the control measure are formulated through directional finite increments and do not require second-order flat derivatives. We further introduce relative semiconvexity along admissible forward-backward trajectories, allowing compensation between the dynamics, running cost, and terminal cost beyond pointwise Hamiltonian convexity. This yields energy dissipation, an O(1/n) convergence rate at the convexity threshold, and geometric convergence when regularisation dominates relative nonconvexity. Explicit LQ criteria and numerical experiments illustrate the scope of the results.

Optimization and Control.title: Continuous-Time Mean-Variance Portfolio Selection Reinforcement Learning Problems for a Markov Regime-Switching System with No-Shorting Constraints
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper is the first to study the continuous-time mean-variance portfolio selection problem with no-shorting constraints in a Markov regime-switching market using reinforcement learning (RL). The main challenge stems from the interaction between random regime shifts and portfolio non-negativity constraints, which typically causes the coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equations to lose smoothness across different state regions. Additionally, directly imposing no-shorting constraints on randomized policies disrupts their analytically tractable Gaussian structure, complicating both exploratory modeling and reinforcement learning. To address these challenges, we propose an auxiliary exploratory approach that limits the policy to a Gaussian distribution and applies the no-shorting constraint solely to its mean. We explicitly characterize the optimal policy for this auxiliary problem and demonstrate that, by appropriately selecting the exploration variance, its optimal mean policy exactly matches the optimal policy of the original constrained mean-variance problem. Building upon this analytical framework, we develop a model-free reinforcement learning algorithm that learns the optimal portfolio policy directly from trajectory data. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results and show that the proposed method can effectively recover the optimal no-shorting portfolio in a regime-switching market.

Optimization and Control.title: Regret-Based Max-Pressure Traffic Signal Control under Uncertain Traffic States
Optimization and Control.summary: Max-pressure (MP) traffic signal control selects phases using pressure scores computed from estimated traffic states, but these states are uncertain and their consequences depend on whether they alter phase ranking and how much pressure is lost. This paper develops a decision-oriented Regret-Based Max-Pressure framework that represents uncertainty through phase-selection regret, defined as the pressure loss of a candidate phase relative to the pressure-maximizing phase under each plausible latent state. We propose Stochastic Regret MP, which minimizes expected regret under a calibrated residual distribution, and Distributionally Robust (DR) Regret MP, which minimizes worst-case expected regret over a Wasserstein ambiguity set. Robustifying regret rather than absolute pressure makes the formulation invariant to state-dependent pressure components shared by all candidate phases, thereby focusing robustness on relative phase quality. We further derive an explicit queue-linear pressure-loss bound and establish strong queue stability when the net-service reserve exceeds the resulting loss coefficient. Numerical experiments show that both methods reduce normalized true-state pressure regret by about 70% relative to Point-estimate MP, while DR Regret MP yields lower network queues than direct robustification of absolute pressure. In microscopic SUMO experiments on a 28-intersection real-world network, Stochastic Regret MP and DR Regret MP reduce mean delay by 18.9% and 14.9%, respectively, and retain benefits under detector undercount and failure. The results show that representing uncertainty through its decision consequences can improve reliable traffic control under imperfect state information.

Optimization and Control.title: On the optimal relaxation parameter of graph-based splitting methods for subspaces
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper, we investigate the behavior of the family of graph-based splitting algorithms specialized to the problem of finding a point in the intersection of linear subspaces. The algorithms in this family, which encompasses several classical methods such as the Douglas-Rachford algorithm, are defined by a connected graph and a subgraph. Our main result establishes that when the graph and subgraph coincide, the optimal relaxation parameter is exactly $1$, thereby extending known results for the Douglas-Rachford algorithm to a much broader class of methods. Our analysis hinges on some properties of iso-averaged linear operators, which are defined as the average of an isometry and the identity, and are characterized by a specific symmetry of the norm of their relaxation.

Optimization and Control.title: A generalized Hurwitz stability criterion via rectangular block Hankel matrices for nonmonic matrix polynomials
Optimization and Control.summary: We develop a Hurwitz stability criterion for nonmonic matrix polynomials via column reduction, generalizing existing approaches constrained by the monic assumption and thus serving as a more natural extension of Gantmacher's classical stability criterion via Markov parameters. Starting from redefining the associated Markov parameters through a column-wise adaptive splitting method, our framework constructs two structured matrices whose rectangular Hankel blocks are obtained via the extraction of these parameters. We establish an explicit interrelation between the inertias of column reduced matrix polynomials and the derived structured matrices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Hurwitz stability of column reduced matrix polynomials can be determined by the Hermitian positive definiteness of these rectangular block Hankel matrices.

Optimization and Control.title: Empirically Calibrated Differential Games for Simulating Driver Interactions
Optimization and Control.summary: Game-theoretic models can resolve vehicle interactions without hand-written priority rules, but whether they describe human drivers once calibrated has rarely been tested. This study formulates a general-sum differential game of vehicle interactions at urban intersections, calibrates it to observed driving, and evaluates it on data not used for calibration. Each vehicle minimizes a cost that combines speed tracking, adherence to a map-derived lane route, control effort, gap keeping based on the intelligent driver model, a predictive conflict term, and a contact barrier, while perceiving the other vehicles with a delay. The game is solved with a feedback iterative linear-quadratic algorithm, and ten behavioral parameters per vehicle are calibrated by Bayesian optimization on trajectories recorded at four intersections in Washington, D.C. The calibrated game reproduces the trajectories of 819 vehicles with a mean position error of 1.00 m. When only each vehicle's route is known, as in a simulator, it is the most accurate of the compared models on 96 held-out vehicles (7.42 m), and ten-fold cross-validation shows that it is significantly more accurate than calibrated SUMO (by 3.61 m), an inverse reinforcement learning model (by 0.93 m), and independent and cooperative variants of the same model (by 0.33 and 0.32 m). The solutions, computed in 2.1 s for a typical interaction, are verified approximate equilibria. Finally, the conflict and steering weights, which the data do not identify, can be set from safety and comfort targets; together with a stiffer contact barrier, this removes the collisions that otherwise occur in 43% of tight closed-loop conflicts.
Optimization and Control.comment: This manuscript is intended for submission to IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems (IEEE T-ITS)

Optimization and Control.title: Stochastic Riccati equations with jumps for indefinite linear-quadratic control: A stochastic value-flow approach
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper studies the nonlinear matrix-valued stochastic Riccati equation with jumps (SRE-J) arising from indefinite stochastic linear-quadratic optimal control problems with random coefficients and Poisson jumps. We demonstrate that the presence of jumps may cause the matrix-valued optimal state process $\mathbf{X}$ to become singular, even under the standard condition. Consequently, the classical representation $P=\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ used in the diffusion case is generally unavailable. To overcome this difficulty, we construct the Riccati process directly from the stochastic value flow under the uniform convexity condition on the cost functional, an approach that requires no invertibility condition on the jump coefficient. We then prove that the SRE-J admits a maximal strongly regular solution, which yields a closed-loop representation of the unique open-loop optimal control. Furthermore, we establish verifiable sufficient conditions for uniform convexity and provide examples of indefinite stochastic linear-quadratic problems with jumps.

Optimization and Control.title: Long Time Behavior and Stabilization for Displacement Monotone Mean Field Games
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper is devoted to the study of the long time behavior of Nash equilibria in Mean Field Games within the framework of displacement monotonicity. We first show that any two equilibria defined on the time horizon $[0,T]$ must be close as $T \to \infty$, in a suitable sense, independently of initial/terminal conditions. The way this stability property is made quantitative involves the $L^2$ distance between solutions of the associated Pontryagin system of FBSDEs that characterizes the equilibria. Therefore, this implies in particular the stability in the 2-Wasserstein distance for the two flows of probability measures describing the agent population density and the $L^2$ distance between the co-states of agents, that are related to the optimal feedback controls. We then prove that the value function of a typical agent converges as $T \to \infty$, and we describe this limit via an infinite horizon MFG system, involving an ergodic constant. All of our convergence results hold true in a unified way for deterministic and idiosyncratic noise driven Mean Field Games, in the case of strongly displacement monotone non-separable Hamiltonians. All these are quantitative at exponential rates.

Optimization and Control.title: Distributed Attacker Assignment and Interception Control in Multi-Agent Target-Attacker-Defender Games
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper addresses the Target-Attacker-Defender (TAD) game within a planar environment, focusing on the protection of a stationary target against incoming threats. To compensate for potential speed disadvantages of the defenders, we leverage geometric pre-positioning within an annular defense perimeter. The problem is formulated as an area interception problem, for which we propose a distributed multi-agent algorithm consisting of two primary modules: target allocation and interception control. For target allocation, an equitable region partitioning strategy is employed to divide the defense area into annular sectors and assign defenders to attackers. Under specified angular-separation and parameter conditions, the proposed partitioning mechanism ensures that each defender is assigned at most one attacker, thereby reducing the complexity of multi-agent assignment. For the control layer, movement protocols based on zero-sum differential games and coverage optimization are designed, achieving Nash equilibrium strategies while maintaining effective barrier coverage. Numerical simulations show that the proposed method enables slower defenders to intercept faster attackers through proactive deployment and maintains nearly constant local computation time as the swarm size increases.

Optimization and Control.title: Online Order Fulfillment with Replenishment
Optimization and Control.summary:
In modern e-commerce and service operations, firms jointly manage inventory replenishment and real-time order fulfillment under demand uncertainty. We study their interaction in a single-resource lost-sales system with heterogeneous rewards, positive lead times, and replenishment cycles of length $T$. A central difficulty is that low regret in one fulfillment cycle need not imply a small profit gap under repeated replenishment, since fulfillment decisions change inventory and, under base-stock replenishment, subsequent orders.
  We consider base-stock and constant-order replenishment and compare online fulfillment with a myopic offline benchmark that knows current-cycle demand but not future demand. We give conditions under which $O(T^α)$ one-cycle regret yields an $O(T^α)$ upper bound on the expected average profit gap, uniformly over all finite horizons $N$. For base stock, the bound remains valid when the online and offline targets are optimized separately. For constant orders, a uniform quadratic count-loss bound gives an unrestricted two-sided comparison between separately optimized systems. For the cycle-restarted Bayes Selector, the finite-horizon bounds are $O(1)$. The optimized long-run constant-order profit gap is also $O(1)$.
  We use these results to compare optimized base stock with greedy fulfillment against optimized constant order with the Bayes Selector and decompose the profit difference into replenishment and fulfillment components. A representative finite-horizon simulation shows that the ranking of the two policy combinations can change with cycle length. We also extend the transfer analysis to multiple resources. Under single-resource base-stock replenishment, a mean-LP quota policy has uniform $O(\sqrt T)$ regret against full-information benchmark.

Optimization and Control.title: Freeform Programmable Liquid Crystal Elastomers via Monolithic Integration of Co-Optimization and 4D-Printing
Optimization and Control.summary: Liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) are active materials capable of large, reversible thermally induced actuation, offering significant potential for applications such as artificial muscles and soft robotics. However, their broader deployment is hindered by the lack of a unified design-to-fabrication framework, the strong coupling among geometry, director fields, and manufacturing constraints, and the difficulty of reliably translating complex designs into physically realizable architectures. Here, we present an autonomous and monolithic integration of co-optimization and 4D printing that enables the end-to-end design-to-realization of versatile programmable LCE architectures with superior precision, complexity, and versatility. The proposed framework establishes a unified design strategy that co-optimizes the freeform multilayer geometry and fully continuous layer-specific director distributions, and subsequently translates the optimized fields into fabrication-ready DIW toolpaths through an automated manufacturing-aware pipeline. To bridge computation and realization, we develop an optimization-centered 4D printing approach with automated, fabrication-aware toolpath generation tailored for direct ink writing of LCEs. With the proposed design-to-fabrication paradigm, we experimentally realize architectures that exhibit complex, non-intuitive thermo-mechanical behaviors. Experiments achieve highly challenging prescribed functionalities beyond the reach of intuition-based approaches and show excellent agreement with numerical simulations across all samples. This work establishes a generalizable inverse design and physical realization of freeform programmable LCE systems, enabling function-oriented and optimization-driven intelligent LCE applications for next-generation soft robotic and responsive material engineering.

Optimization and Control.title: A branch-and-filter method for mixed-integer linear programming
Optimization and Control.summary: We develop a new tree-search framework for mixed-integer linear programming problems, which incorporates a filter mechanism as a node-acceptance device. The introduced branch-and-filter algorithm combines proper branching actions with a filter on integrality violation and an incumbent-dependent objective coordinate. Inspired by classical filter methods in nonconvex constrained optimization, the proposed method moves to a restoration phase whenever sufficient progress cannot be provided by the filter and funnel mechanisms, the latter of which is anchored at global relaxation lower bounds. Under mild assumptions, the introduced method either certifies infeasibility in finitely many iterations, or converges to global optimality. Moreover, we establish a total outer iteration complexity bound of order $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-1})$ to certification of an $\varepsilon$-optimal mixed-integer solution through fixed-integer linear programming recovery. We finally perform several numerical experiments to study the performance of branch-and-filter against benchmark solvers, under a branch-and-bound, a branch-and-cut, and a novel cell-deletion realization of the proposed restoration oracle.

Optimization and Control.title: Convex Analysis of Relaxation Dynamics in Chemical Reaction Networks and Generalized Gradient Flows
Optimization and Control.summary: We obtain bounds on the Kullback--Leibler divergence to equilibrium for mass-action chemical reaction networks (CRNs) with equilibrium. The associated trajectory-dependent bounds are characterized in terms of the singular values of the stoichiometric matrix, convexity parameters, and time-integrated activities via deformed-exponential-type functions. We further extend these bounds within a generalized gradient flow framework. We highlight the biological relevance of this framework: the resulting bounds apply to quasi-steady-state regimes, where long transients and plateau-like behavior are common and functionally important. We illustrate the framework using a catalytic CRN exhibiting plateaus, where the bounds provide an a posteriori characterization of slow relaxation induced by local convexity and provide a bound-based approach to quantifying relaxation in CRNs.
Optimization and Control.comment: 34 pages, 5 figures (Main Text); 11 pages, 5 figures (Supplementary Material). Accepted for publication in SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics

Optimization and Control.title: Optimization with Parametric Variational Inequality Constraints on a Moving Set Based on a Smoothing Method
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper focuses on optimization problems constrained by Parametric Variational Inequalities (PVI) defined on a moving set. Unlike most existing works on mathematical programs with equilibrium constraints, the equilibrium constraints have parameters not only in the function but also in the related set. We show that the solution function of the PVI is Lipschitz continuous with respect to the upper-level decision variables and the solution set of the optimization problem is nonempty and bounded. Moreover, we prove that the metric regularity of the constraints holds automatically, which allows us to characterize stationary points without any additional assumptions. A Smoothing Implicit Gradient Algorithm (SIGA) is proposed based on the smoothing approximation of the PVI with a novel scheme for updating the smoothing parameter. We prove the convergence of SIGA to a stationary point and validate the efficiency of SIGA by numerical examples from synthetic problems and portfolio management with real data.

Optimization and Control.title: Timed Recovery Safe Gradient Flows for Constrained Nonlinear Programming
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper studies how to relax pointwise feasibility in continuous-time dynamics for inequality-constrained nonlinear programming while retaining a quantitative feasible-recovery guarantee. Existing safe gradient flows enforce forward invariance of the feasible set, which yields an anytime-feasible dynamics but can be overly restrictive for optimization because it suppresses transient infeasible motion that may be essential for effective descent. To address this limitation, we propose a timed recovery safe gradient flow that replaces pointwise feasibility with fixed-horizon feasible recovery. The proposed construction augments the state with a timer that records the elapsed infeasible duration and computes a minimum-norm correction to the nominal gradient flow through a pointwise convex quadratic program. We show that the resulting augmented safe set is forward invariant and that every trajectory initialized from the feasible set returns to it within every time window of length \(τ\). We further show that, in a strict interior inactive regime, the closed-loop dynamics reduces exactly to the nominal gradient flow and recovers the corresponding local convergence behavior. Numerical examples illustrate how the recovery horizon shapes the closed-loop behavior and corroborate the theoretical analysis.
Optimization and Control.comment: 15 pages. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control in May 2026

Optimization and Control.title: Transient Amplification in Cascaded Gradient Methods: Exact Minimax Laws and Tracking without Resonance
Optimization and Control.summary: Leader-follower gradient iterations, including bilevel and two-time-scale methods, can exhibit large finite-time excursions despite asymptotic stability. For cascaded iterations with block matrix J = [[A,0],[C,D]], symmetric diagonal blocks of norm at most gamma < 1, and coupling norm at most c, we prove an exact, dimension-free minimax formula: at every horizon t, the worst-case amplification equals the spectral norm of [[gamma^t,0],[c t gamma^(t-1),gamma^t]], attained by an aligned two-dimensional quadratic. Consequently, the worst transient is on the order of 1 + c/(1-gamma), and eigenvalues alone cannot predict finite-time gain. Under martingale noise, the aligned system has stationary follower variance sigma^2 c^2 (1+gamma^2)/(1-gamma^2)^3, establishing cubic inverse-gap scaling. For quadratic followers, the coupling is linked to follower sensitivity R by C = (I-D)R. When the leader is isotropic and the follower map is positive semidefinite, amplification is at most 1 plus the operator norm of R, independently of the spectral gaps. A look-ahead Newton update eliminates follower memory and is minimax-optimal among linear updates that track the leader exactly. Experiments validate the bounds and show that accelerated or inexact follower solvers can exceed the sensitivity bound when their effective maps have negative eigenvalues. Code and experiment scripts: https://github.com/Axym-Labs/transient-amplification

Optimization and Control.title: Continuous-Time Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Control: Limits, Duality, and Stability
Optimization and Control.summary: A sampled robust control problem averages future values over disturbance laws, while its continuous-time counterpart evolves with an averaged drift. We establish a fluid limit connecting these two models for Wasserstein ambiguity sets. Under a uniform disturbance moment bound and subcritical growth, sampled Bellman values converge locally uniformly to the upper and lower values of a discounted differential game. The argument accommodates unbounded disturbances without requiring square-integrable increments. We also derive an explicit bound on the change in either game value when both the radius and center of the ambiguity set vary. For Euclidean disturbance space, uniform Lipschitz continuity in the disturbance, common state and cost Lipschitz bounds, and a discount rate exceeding the drift's state Lipschitz constant, this estimate converts distributional confidence bounds into uniform value approximation bounds. Static Wasserstein duality reformulates pointwise distributional optimization; affine disturbance dependence permits an exact reduction to a ball of means. Experiments illustrate the common limit and decreasing value error with sample size. For a nonlinear disturbance model, uniform shifts overestimate worst-case recovery speed by about 36\%. In a two-product inventory model, increasing ambiguity raises production near balance while reducing the region of full production in deeper backlogs.

Optimization and Control.title: Approximate Bregman proximal gradient algorithm with variable metric Armijo line search
Optimization and Control.summary: We propose a variant of the approximate Bregman proximal gradient (ABPG) algorithm for minimizing the sum of a smooth nonconvex function and a nonsmooth convex function. ABPG is known to converge globally to a stationary point even when the smooth part of the objective function does not have a globally Lipschitz continuous gradient, and its iterates can often be expressed in closed form. However, ABPG relies on an Armijo line search to guarantee global convergence, which can slow down its practical performance. To address this issue, we propose a variant of ABPG with a variable metric Armijo line search, which relaxes the Armijo condition. We prove that the line search terminates in finitely many steps for a general nonsmooth convex function. Under the variable metric Armijo condition, we establish global subsequential convergence of the algorithm. Moreover, assuming the Kurdyka--Łojasiewicz property, we also prove that the algorithm globally converges to a stationary point. Numerical experiments on $\ell_p$-regularized least squares problems, nonnegative linear inverse problems and phase retrieval demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing algorithms.

Optimization and Control.title: MeshCone: Second-Order Cone Programming for Geometrically-Constrained Mesh Enhancement
Optimization and Control.summary: Modern mesh generation pipelines whether learning-based or classical often produce outputs requiring post-processing to achieve production-quality geometry. This work introduces MeshCone, a convex optimization framework for guided mesh refinement that leverages reference geometry to correct deformed or degraded meshes. We formulate the problem as a second-order cone program where vertex positions are optimized to align with target geometry while enforcing smoothness through convex edge-length regularization. MeshCone performs geometry-aware optimization that preserves fine details while correcting structural defects. We demonstrate robust performance across 56 diverse object categories from ShapeNet and ThreeDScans, achieving superior refinement quality compared to Laplacian smoothing and unoptimized baselines while maintaining sub-second inference times. MeshCone is particularly suited for applications where reference geometry is available, such as mesh-from-template workflows, scan-to-CAD alignment, and quality assurance in asset production pipelines.
Optimization and Control.comment: This submission has been withdrawn by the authors. Upon further review, we identified issues in the analysis that require significant revision. An updated and more thoroughly developed version will be submitted once these have been resolved

Optimization and Control.title: A Dynamic Inventory Rationing Model for Last-Mile Delivery of Medication in Liberia's Community Health Program
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the dynamic allocation of scarce medications in Liberia's community health program. A central warehouse supplies a health facility and the Community Health Assistants (CHAs) it supervises. When a CHA runs out of medication, patients are referred to the facility, incurring travel costs if they complete the referral and remain untreated otherwise. Allocating inventory to CHAs allows more patients to receive treatment without traveling, while retaining inventory centrally preserves flexibility to respond to uncertain demand. The allocation problem must balance these considerations while accounting for fairness across locations. We formulate this problem as a finite-horizon stochastic control problem whose objective combines the costs of referrals and untreated patients with a demand-weighted fairness utility. Because standard dynamic programming methods are computationally intractable in this setting, we develop a continuous-time approximation that involves controlling the drift rate of a reflected Brownian motion. We then adapt the deep splitting method, using deep neural networks to approximate the value function and its gradient and compute a dynamic allocation policy. We calibrate the model using data on malaria cases among children in the Fangonda region of Lofa County, Liberia, and evaluate the proposed policy in the original discrete-time model. In the baseline setting, our policy reduces operating costs by about 6% relative to the strongest benchmark, the fairness-only policy, while retaining approximately 98% of its fairness utility. Additional experiments show that higher referral costs shift inventory toward CHAs and reduce local unmet demand, while greater demand variability increases our policy's performance over the fairness-only benchmark. Our model and computational approach provide a framework for studying similar last-mile allocation problems.

Optimization and Control.title: On Exact Critical-Region Boundaries in Continuous-Time Multiparametric Optimal Control Problems
Optimization and Control.summary: Continuous-time multiparametric model predictive control solves the optimal control problem once, offline, for every initial state, and divides the initial-state space into critical regions, each with its own control law and sequence of active constraints. A boundary between two regions is either a hyperplane, given by one linear equation, or curved. The curved boundaries have not been computed to date; a classifier has been trained instead to distinguish the regions, so the partition has been known only approximately. In this paper we show that a curved boundary can be computed exactly, without solving any optimal control problem. The method rests on one property. Once the sequence of active constraints is fixed, together with the instants inside it at which a constraint becomes active or inactive (the switching times) and the instant at which the change of the neighboring region first appears (the event time), every condition on a boundary is a linear equation in the initial state, so the computation of a boundary, curved or not, is exact. We fix one of these instants, a switching time or the event time, and solve the linear equations that correspond to it for the corresponding initial state on the boundary; stepping the fixed instant along the horizon yields the whole boundary. A hyperplane is the case in which no instant is left to fix. We illustrate the method on the Newell-Lee evaporator, which has seven critical regions and eight boundaries, four hyperplanes and four curved, computing one boundary of each type in full with the adjacent regions at its ends.

Optimization and Control.title: The BAR-SOT Method: Long-term Average Cost Control as Stochastic Optimal Self-Transport
