In the special case of linear systems, the proposed MPC formulation reduces to a quadratic program, and the offline design and online computational complexity are only marginally increased compared to a nominal design. Numerical examples demonstrate benefits compared to state-of-the-art soft-constrained MPC formulations.
Optimization and Control.comment: Extended version of accepted paper in Automatica. Appendix contains additional details

Optimization and Control.title: A Two-Stage Optimization Framework for Real-World Large-Scale University Course Timetabling Based on Orthogonalized Hierarchical Modeling and Conflict-Driven ALNS Repair
Optimization and Control.summary: University course timetabling is a large-scale combinatorial optimization problem involving strongly coupled temporal and resource constraints. This paper proposes a two-stage optimization framework for real-world large-scale university course timetabling, integrating orthogonalized hierarchical modeling with conflict-driven adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) repair. The first stage performs global course-level optimization, while the second identifies residual conflicts through a conflict graph and localizes them into connected conflict regions. The Course--Occurrence--Session representation provides the structural basis for multi-granularity repair, which employs Cluster-, Course-, Occurrence-, and Session-level destroy operators within the ALNS framework, followed by fine-grained greedy repair. The framework is evaluated on a real-world university timetabling instance involving 3,073 course groups, 8,015 scheduling events, 998 student classes, and 1,511 instructors. Ablation experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of hierarchical repair granularity and adaptive operator selection. Across ten independent runs, the ALNS + Greedy framework achieves a mean residual conflict count of 18.50, compared with 172 for deterministic Greedy-only repair under the same initial scheduling conditions, representing an 89.24\% reduction. These results support the effectiveness of the proposed conflict-driven hierarchical repair framework for large-scale university course timetabling.

Optimization and Control.title: A derivative-free trust-region approach for Low Order-Value Optimization problems
Optimization and Control.summary: The Low Order-Value Optimization (LOVO) problem involves minimizing the minimum among a finite number of function values within a feasible set. LOVO has several practical applications such as robust parameter estimation, protein alignment, portfolio optimization, among others. In this work, we are interested in the constrained nonlinear optimization LOVO problem of minimizing the minimum between a finite number of function values subject to a nonempty closed convex set where each function is a black-box and continuously differentiable, but the derivatives are not available. We develop the first derivative-free trust-region algorithm for constrained LOVO problems with convergence to weakly critical points. Under suitable conditions, we establish the global convergence of the algorithm and also its worst-case iteration complexity analysis. An initial open-source implementation using only linear interpolation models is developed. Extensive numerical experiments and comparison with existing alternatives show the properties and the efficiency of the proposed approach when solving LOVO problems.

Optimization and Control.title: Observer-Based Event-Triggered Control of Infinite-Dimensional Linear Systems
Optimization and Control.summary:
We investigate observer-based event-triggered stabilization of infinite-dimensional linear systems, such as those governed by partial differential equations. A Luenberger observer and a feedback gain are assumed to stabilize the closed loop in continuous time, and we study what happens when the control input is only updated at instants generated by a dynamic event-triggering mechanism. Unlike approaches that rely on state-dependent triggering rules, our condition only involves the observer state and the measured output, which makes it implementable when the full state is not measured. It compares the deviation of a monitored signal of the observer since the last update with a threshold made of two parts. The first one is a relative part, proportional to the current size of this signal, and the second one is a positive internal variable, which does not depend on the observer state. In particular, the case where the threshold reduces to the internal variable alone is covered.
  Under suitable assumptions, we establish the well-posedness of the closed-loop system and the absence of Zeno behavior for general choices of these two parts, and we prove its exponential stability under a small-gain condition on the relative part. We further analyse the existence of a dwell-time, namely a positive lower bound on the time elapsed between two consecutive triggering instants. When the sampled dynamics is bounded, as in finite-dimensional systems or systems with a finite-dimensional unstable part, we obtain a dwell-time independent of the initial data, together with exponential stability. For unbounded generators, we exhibit a system satisfying all our assumptions for which no triggering rule can achieve both a dwell-time independent of the initial data and bounded trajectories.

Optimization and Control.title: Robust global supply chain reconfiguration under tariff and geopolitical uncertainty
Optimization and Control.summary: Global supply chains are increasingly exposed to trade policy shocks and physical disruptions arising from common geopolitical events. We develop a robust optimization framework with two decision stages for strategic supply chain reconfiguration. Supplier qualification and transportation arc activation decisions are made before uncertainty is realized, while operational flows adapt afterward. Geopolitical uncertainty is represented through country level shocks that can jointly trigger tariff escalation, policy induced restrictions on cross border capacity, facility disruptions, and physical transportation failures. The resulting min max min problem is reformulated by dualizing the operational recourse problem, yielding a nonconvex mixed integer bilinear adversarial problem solved within a column and constraint generation procedure. Comparison with complete enumeration verifies the implementation on small instances, while experiments on 60 synthetic supply chain networks of varying sizes assess computational performance. The results show that omitting geopolitical transmission channels during strategic design can lead to substantial deterioration in cost and service under full geopolitical stress. Broader protection is achieved primarily through changes in transportation network configuration rather than increased supplier qualification. Robust performance also depends on the severity and composition of geopolitical consequences, with restrictions on cross border capacity exerting a stronger effect than comparable proportional changes in tariff severity over the tested ranges. A geographically grounded case analysis further shows that the value of individual uncertainty channels depends on network structure and geographic exposure.

Optimization and Control.title: Logic-Based Benders Decomposition for Time Slot Management with Mixed Logit Demand
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper develops an exact solution framework for the choice-based time slot management problem under mixed logit demand in attended home delivery systems. The problem jointly optimizes delivery slot offerings, price discounts, and routing decisions, with customer choices endogenously modeled through a simulation-based mixed logit formulation embedded via sample average approximation, resulting in a large-scale stochastic mixed-integer program. To address this complexity, we propose a logic-based Benders decomposition (LBBD) that separates strategic assortment and pricing decisions, together with customer choice, from scenario-specific vehicle routing subproblems. We derive problem-specific optimality cuts that exploit the routing structure to provide stronger bounds than generic cuts, and establish their validity. To enhance computational performance, we introduce and systematically evaluate several strengthening strategies, including relaxation-based cut generation and capacity- and flow-based valid inequalities. We further compare two equivalent encodings of the embedded choice model and show that the relative value of each strengthening strategy depends on the strength of the master formulation it complements. Computational experiments on benchmark instances show that the proposed framework significantly extends the range of solvable instances compared to direct MILP approaches. The framework is exact: it converges to a proven optimal solution given sufficient time, and the bounds it produces at intermediate iterations are valid. Within a 12-hour limit, proven optimality is reached for instances with up to 10 customers, and valid bounds are obtained up to 40 customers, including sizes at which the direct MILP formulation returns no feasible solution.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Minimum Speed for a Fire Blocking Problem
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider a dynamic blocking problem: a fire, starting on a bounded open set $R_0\subset\mathbb R^2$, propagates in the plane with unit speed in all directions. To block it, a barrier can be constructed in real time, at speed $λ>0$. A long standing conjecture by the first author states that the fire can be entirely surrounded by the barrier, in finite time, if and only if $λ>2$. The present paper improves on earlier lower bounds. Namely, if $λ\leq Λ=1.62621170228\ldots $ we show that the fire cannot be blocked. We also prove that, if $λ\leq 2$, the fire cannot be blocked by constructing a barrier which is a simple closed curve. More precisely, if the barrier does not contain purely delaying arcs, i.e.~arcs which are eventually surrounded by the fire on both sides, then for $λ<2$ the region burned by the fire at time $t>0$ has area $A(t)>(2-λ)t^2/4$.

Optimization and Control.title: A Search-Based Algorithm for Multistage Robust Discrete Linear Optimization and its Implementation
Optimization and Control.summary: Robust optimization models that allow decisions to adapt to newly revealed information remain computationally challenging and are often limited to two decision stages or are addressed heuristically or via approximation schemes. This challenge is further amplified when uncertainty sets depend on earlier decisions. Conventional approaches to such problems often require problem-specific reformulations and tailored algorithms, highlighting the need for an exact model-and-run approach. We address this gap by presenting an algorithmic framework for solving multistage robust discrete linear optimization problems. This exact approach adapts and integrates ideas from game-tree search, quantified conflict-driven clause learning, and integer linear programming to explore the minimax tree and is implemented in the open-source solver Yasol. The solver supports discrete decision variables across multiple stages, discrete uncertainty sets with polyhedral or decision-dependent structure, and mixed-integer recourse in the final stage. It can be used as a standalone executable or through a C++ library interface, allowing it to serve as a reference solver for exact methods in multistage robust discrete linear optimization. In an extensive computational study, we demonstrate the capabilities of our solver. The results show competitive performance against a reference approach from the literature for a protection-interdiction problem, as well as strong performance on bilevel benchmark instances. For a multistage cutting-stock problem, we demonstrate the substantial loss in solution quality that can arise from neglecting the multistage structure and show that our solver significantly outperforms decision-rule approximations in terms of computational efficiency while certifying the true multistage optimum.

Optimization and Control.title: RoRo stowage planning: a systematic study of mathematical formulations
Optimization and Control.summary: Stowage planning for Roll-On/Roll-Off (RoRo) vessels can be represented with different mathematical formulations for efficient stowage plans: hybrid-slot, grid-based, and lane-based representations. In this work, we implement and compare three formulations equally across a diverse set of instances. We extend these three representations to handle heterogeneous cargo in terms of size and weight, and to address advanced stability requirements, such as centre of gravity limits, stress force limits, and ballast-water adjustments. We evaluate the models in three configurations: cargo placement, simple stability with centres of gravity limits and ballast adjustments, and full stability, which adds shear-force and bending-moment limits. The tests are conducted on three different vessel sizes and solved with a mixed-integer programming solver. The hybrid-slot and grid-based models both perform well finding solutions for 447 out of 486 instances across all configurations; however, the hybrid-slot model placed 8% more cargo than the grid model. By contrast, the lane model only finds solutions for 142 instances and placed 15% less cargo than the grid-based model. The solutions generated by the hybrid-slot model are validated using a commercial vessel-stability software to verify our stability estimations, showing issues in only 24 of 162 instances, which are easily avoided by tightening the stability constraints. Finally, we address the placement of hazardous and refrigerated cargo in an efficient manner for the hybrid-slot model by employing lazy constraints which is shown to solve realistic sized instances.

Optimization and Control.title: Theoretical and Computational Advances in Birkhoff Pseudospectral Transcription for Aerospace Optimal Control
Optimization and Control.summary: Birkhoff pseudospectral methods replace the differentiation matrices of classical transcriptions with integration operators whose conditioning does not deteriorate with polynomial order. This paper presents theoretical and computational advancements toward their practical use in aerospace optimal control. The initial-point-anchored Birkhoff integration operator is constructed explicitly for flipped Legendre-Gauss-Radau grids and related exactly to the corresponding Lagrange differentiation matrix and, through a reflection, to the standard Radau Birkhoff operator, whose conditioning properties it inherits. Rate constraints on nonlinear functions of states and controls are enforced directly through the pseudospectral operators and, for control-rate limits, shown to be primal and dual equivalent to state augmentation. Non-affine time mappings concentrate the nodes around localized trajectory features, and composing affine scaling and equilibration transformations provides a systematic way to construct scaling strategies. The methods are implemented in the open-source MATLAB framework RAPTOR and tested across a range of challenging optimal control problems, including a dense-grid orbit-raising problem, a rate-limited landing scenario, a Space Shuttle entry problem, and a five-phase reusable-launch-vehicle mission.

Optimization and Control.title: Unified Communication Compression Beyond Global Error Bounds for Distributed Nonconvex Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper, we propose a unified compression algorithm for distributed nonconvex opitmization with both the locally- and globally-bounded communication compressors, including 1-bit compressors, saturating quantizers, and the globally-bounded compressors with both relative and absolute compression errors, as well as additional arbitrary bounded noise. We provide a rigorous convergence analysis in nonconvex settings and establish linear convergence under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz (P-L) condition. Notably, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence rate for the locally-bounded class in the distributed nonconvex setting, matching that achieved by the centralized algorithms with 1-bit compressors, where $T$ denotes the total number of iterations. Moreover, one initial uncompressed communication round further yields an order-wise improvement to $\mathcal{O}(1/T^{2/3})$. For the P-L setting and the globally-bounded class, we recover state-of-the-art convergence rates.

Optimization and Control.title: Conditional Sampling via Wasserstein Autoencoders and Triangular Transport
Optimization and Control.summary: We present Conditional Wasserstein Autoencoders (CWAEs), a framework for conditional simulation that exploits low-dimensional structure in both the conditioned and the conditioning variables. The key idea is to modify a Wasserstein autoencoder to use a (block-) triangular decoder and impose an appropriate independence assumption on the latent variables. We show that the resulting model gives an autoencoder that can exploit low-dimensional structure while simultaneously the decoder can be used for conditional simulation. We explore various theoretical properties of CWAEs, including their connections to conditional optimal transport (OT) problems. We also present alternative formulations that lead to three architectural variants forming the foundation of our algorithms. We present a series of numerical experiments that demonstrate that our different CWAE variants achieve substantial reductions in approximation error relative to the low-rank ensemble Kalman filter (LREnKF), particularly in problems where the support of the conditional measures is truly low-dimensional.
Optimization and Control.comment: Accepted to the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026). 8 pages, 5 figures

Optimization and Control.title: Regularization and Full Support for the CBO Equation with Measure Initial Data
Optimization and Control.summary: We prove global well-posedness and regularization for the isotropic consensus-based optimization equation with initial probability measures of finite fourth moment. Under suitable weight decay assumptions, after any nonconstant consensus motion, both the density and the consensus trajectory become smooth, and all spatial Sobolev norms are locally bounded in time. The proof uses a Fourier commutator estimate, localization and iteration, followed by a nonlinear time bootstrap. Counterexamples show that smoothing can fail at a stationary consensus point. For non-Dirac initial data, we also prove positivity away from the consensus point and full support at every positive time in all dimensions.
Optimization and Control.comment: add remark 1.4 and expand the introduction

Optimization and Control.title: Verifying Control Invariance of H-Polytopes is coNP-Complete
Optimization and Control.summary: We prove that verifying whether an H-polytope is control invariant for a discrete-time linear system with polytopic input constraints is \textsc{coNP}-complete. This establishes a fundamental computational complexity barrier for set-theoretic control. As an immediate consequence, the exact computation of maximal control invariant subsets of H-polytopes is \textsc{coNP}-hard. These hardness results hold regardless of whether the input constraint set is given in H- or V-representation.

Optimization and Control.title: Frequency-Uniform Log-Regret Reinforcement Learning for Diffusions
Optimization and Control.summary: High-frequency control problems are often studied through time discretization, but refining the timestep $δ$ increases the discrete horizon $H=T/δ$ and can make standard finite-horizon regret guarantees deteriorate even when the physical horizon $T$ is fixed. We study episodic value-based reinforcement learning for Euler discretizations of controlled diffusions. The performance is measured as the cumulative regret over $K$ episodes relative to the optimal policy of the corresponding Euler model. Under stability and regularity conditions on value function gradients, Bellman residual derivatives, and fitted critics, we prove an $\mathcal{O}(\log K)$ regret bound with constants uniform in $δ$. For dynamics with drift linear in unknown parameters and unknown constant diffusion covariance, we verify localized versions of these conditions for a constrained, model-based controlled-diffusion fitted-$Q$ algorithm (CD-FQ) and obtain high-probability $\mathcal{O}(\log K\log\log K)$ regret for fixed and finite $T$, again with constants uniform in $δ$.

Optimization and Control.title: Momentum in large-batch training: Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, Nesterov improves data efficiency
Optimization and Control.summary: We study when and how momentum improves large-batch training in the one-pass regime, using power-law kernel regression as a tractable setting. We first characterize stochastic stability through the \emph{critical learning rate}, defined as the largest learning rate for stable training, and obtain $η_{\mathrm{SGD}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim 1$, $η_{\mathrm{Polyak}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim \min\{1,B(1-β)\}$, and $η_{\mathrm{Nesterov}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim \min\{1,B^q(1-β)\}$, where $B$ is the batch size, $β\in[0,1)$ is the momentum factor, and \(q>1\) is the capacity exponent governing spectral decay. Within the stable region, we derive scaling laws for the full risk dynamics, capturing the progression from an early transient through power-law decay to a noise floor. We then optimize the final-step risk under a fixed data budget, obtaining a three-regime phase diagram that reveals how the benefits of momentum change with batch size. Notably, Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, the largest batch size preserving the optimal small-batch data-scaling exponent, thereby allowing fewer sequential updates without sacrificing data efficiency. In contrast, Nesterov improves the optimal data-scaling exponent in the large-batch regime through look-ahead-induced suppression of noise amplification. Experiments on PLK regression quantitatively support the theoretical scaling predictions, while neural-network experiments provide qualitative evidence for the predicted batch-size dependence and stability behavior.
Optimization and Control.comment: 63 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Revised proofs; added neural-network experiments

Optimization and Control.title: Robust Log-Contrast Regression for High-Dimensional Compositional Microbiome Data with Outliers
Optimization and Control.summary: It is well known that microbiome sequencing data are naturally compositional and often have a complex subcomposition structure, as well as a lot of noise and some outliers. These characteristics make classical log-contrast regression difficult to apply, because it is sensitive to extreme values and cannot fully meet the linear constraints of compositional predictors. To tackle these issues, in this paper, we propose a robust log-contrast regression framework that incorporates the Huber loss function along with a Lasso penalty, which not only boosts resistance to outliers but also facilitates sparse variable selection. It is important to note that the general linear constraints, which are explicitly imposed, serve to preserve the algebraic coherence of compositional and subcompositional covariates. Under some mild assumptions, we theoretically prove that the proposed method achieves non-asymptotic guarantees in finite samples, comparable to those of Huber loss estimators, ensuring robustness. To implement the method efficiently, we develop a symmetric Gauss--Seidel-based alternating direction method of multipliers based on its dual formulation with a convergence guarantee, and it is also easy to implement in the sense that each subproblem admits a closed-form solution. To evaluate the statistical performance of the proposed method, we conduct a series of numerical experiments using simulated data and gut microbiome data, which show that the proposed method achieves better estimation accuracy, competitive prediction performance, and more reliable outlier identification than the benchmark method RobRegCC.

Optimization and Control.title: Error analysis and optimal sample allocation for randomized unbiased estimation: the single term estimator
Optimization and Control.summary: Randomized unbiased estimation can be highly efficient for approximating expectations of functionals of stochastic differential equations. However, in practice, the optimal computational efficiency is rarely attained due to errors arising from parameter estimation and truncation. The effects of these errors on computational efficiency have not been investigated. In this article, we study the error analysis and optimal sample allocation for the single term estimator. Specifically, under mild assumptions on the estimated parameters, we develop a unified error analysis that incorporates both sources of error, and establish the relevant convergence rates for the computational efficiency loss. Based on this analysis, we further investigate the optimal allocation of the computational budget for parameter estimation, and propose several efficient sample allocation strategies. Numerical experiments support the theoretical convergence rates and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Pontryagin Maximum Principle for Rough Stochastic Differential Equations
Optimization and Control.summary: We establish first- and second-order Pontryagin (a.k.a. stochastic) maximum principles for rough stochastic control problems with general nonlinear $\mathrm{Lip}^γ$-rough vector fields. This complements the dynamic programming approach of Friz-Lê-Zhang [FLZ26b], and extends the maximum principle of Horst-Zhang [HZ26] beyond affine rough vector fields. The paper concludes with applications to pathwise stochastic optimal control.

Optimization and Control.title: Perturbed Gradient Descent Algorithms are Small-Disturbance Input-to-State Stable
Optimization and Control.summary: This article investigates the robustness of gradient descent algorithms under perturbations. The concept of small-disturbance input-to-state stability (ISS) for discrete-time nonlinear dynamical systems is introduced, along with its Lyapunov characterization. The conventional linear Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition is then extended to a nonlinear version, and it is shown that the gradient descent algorithm is small-disturbance ISS provided the objective function satisfies the generalized nonlinear PL condition. This small-disturbance ISS property guarantees that the gradient descent algorithm converges to a small neighborhood of the optimum under sufficiently small perturbations. As a direct application of the developed framework, we demonstrate that the LQR cost satisfies the generalized nonlinear PL condition, thereby establishing that the policy gradient algorithm for LQR is small-disturbance ISS. Additionally, other popular policy gradient algorithms, including natural policy gradient and Gauss-Newton method, are also proven to be small-disturbance ISS.

Optimization and Control.title: Axiomatic Learning and Probabilistic Structures with first applications to variants of Arithmetic Machine Learning and beyond
Optimization and Control.summary: We introduce the Axiomatic Learning Structures (ALS) and Axiomatic Probabilistic Structure (APS) in order to study the interactions of Machine Learning, Optimization, with research frameworks- which, we take the view, can be characterized at the core by the corresponding axioms. The ALS explores the interplays between structures that one is interested in Learning Theory such as Loss functions and the axioms of the objects and transformations involved in these functions. The APS studies the interaction between structures of interest in Probability Theory such as Gibbs distributions, equations with noise, etc. and the axioms of the corresponding objects and transformations. We also introduce in Section 6 Transformations-Axiomatic Based Learning (TABLe) on Mathematical data-sets. One feature of this approach is the ranking of transformations from a table for a certain task based on scores which reflect which transformations work better than others, similarly to when human investigators try various methods on a task. We also study structure recovery from noisy data. In particular, to exemplify the ideas, we consider loss functions which contain derivations and derivations-like transformations. As a first application we study recovery in the context of polynomials with integer coefficients using standard derivatives along with other types of derivations which appear in Arithmetic: the p-derivations which satisfy \textit{different axioms} from the usual derivatives. As a first application of the APS we study a class of noisy (partial/mixed) derivations equations. In the last sections, to provide further potential applications of this framework, we give an overview of an initial simplified Opinion Dynamics model and its (simultaneous) study of rules of updates.

Optimization and Control.title: Data-Driven Distributionally Robust Planning of Coastal Distribution Networks and PV-Storage-EV Stations for Low-Carbon Energy Transition
Optimization and Control.summary: Coastal distribution networks (DNs) are becoming key infrastructure for the low-carbon energy transition as electric vehicle (EV) charging, photovoltaic (PV) generation, energy storage, and marine renewable procurement are increasingly coupled at the planning stage. Existing planning models, however, usually treat network expansion, PV-storage-EV station (PSES) deployment, low-carbon operation, and coastal asset degradation separately. This paper proposes a data-driven distributionally robust planning framework for coastal DNs and PSESs. The framework jointly optimizes radial network topology and PSES siting while incorporating salt-spray degradation costs, carbon-emission-flow (CEF)-based nodal carbon accounting, and tidal-generation-driven procurement costs. To represent heterogeneous uncertainty, the model combines continuous box uncertainty for load and PV availability with probability ambiguity over EV-charging scenarios generated from historical charging profiles. The resulting two-stage distributionally robust optimization problem is reformulated through exact relaxation of ESS mode binaries and KKT-based decomposition, and is solved by an inexact column-and-constraint generation (i-C&CG) algorithm. Case studies on a realistic 47-node coastal feeder show that salt-spray exposure can alter the selected topology and PSES siting, while the proposed planning scheme improves voltage quality, reduces annualized total cost, and reveals the cost--carbon trade-off of tidal procurement. The tailored i-C&CG algorithm obtains the same optimal design as conventional C&CG with about an order-of-magnitude reduction in solution time.

Optimization and Control.title: Wasserstein approximation of measures via orthogonal frames: statistical and computational complexities
Optimization and Control.summary: Dimension-reduction methods such as PCA identify a subspace capturing most of the variation in the data, but not a distinguished basis within it. Selecting a basis in which the samples are sparsely represented is a recurring task in unsupervised learning, addressed by methods in factor analysis, dictionary learning, and subspace clustering. We pose this task as Wasserstein approximation of the data distribution by measures supported on the axes of an orthogonal frame, which, in turn, reduces to a nonsmooth optimization problem over the orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}(d)$. We show that, under mild assumptions, both empirical risk minimizers and a locally initialized stochastic gradient method recover the population-optimal frame at the near-parametric rate $\widetilde{O}_d(n^{-1/2})$, where $n$ is the sample size. The main difficulty is that, although the population objective is smooth, the empirical objective is not-this mismatch precludes standard covering arguments. We overcome this issue by replacing Lipschitz continuity of the empirical gradient with a coarsely Lipschitz bound, a tool that may be of independent interest. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings.

Optimization and Control.title: QESChunker: A Single Objective Unifies Overlapping and Non-Overlapping Chunking for RAG
Optimization and Control.summary: Chunking is a fundamental preprocessing step in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), yet most existing chunkers rely primarily on heuristics. We introduce the Question--Evidence-Supervised Chunker (QESChunker), to our knowledge the first method for constructing static chunk indices from question--evidence supervision. QESChunker constructs document-specific chunk indices by optimizing over human-annotated or LLM-generated question--evidence pairs, without access to held-out test queries. We formulate non-overlapping and overlapping index construction through a unified question--evidence utility-maximization objective, turning chunking into a supervised combinatorial optimization problem. Under the non-overlap constraint, the objective decomposes over chunks and can be optimized exactly in polynomial time by dynamic programming. When overlap is allowed, the objective becomes monotone submodular; exact optimization is NP-hard, but our greedy achieves a $(1-1/\sqrt{e})$-approximation. Across two self-constructed and three public datasets, both variants outperform existing chunking methods in complete-evidence recall in nearly all evaluated settings, under the same overlap regime and a fixed hybrid retriever. These results recast chunking as supervised, budget-aware index construction for evidence retrieval.

Optimization and Control.title: NextEval: An Agent-Based Solver and Benchmark for Derivative-Free Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: Derivative-free optimization (DFO) addresses problems where derivatives are unavailable or costly to obtain. This setting often arises in simulation-based and experimental applications, where evaluating the black-box objective can itself be costly. Thus, it remains a central challenge in DFO to effectively exploit accumulated observations to select informative evaluation points under a limited budget. In this light, we introduce the NextEval solver, an agent-based DFO solver, which integrates the capabilities of a large language model (LLM) to guide the sequential selection of evaluation points. Specifically, we establish a system that combines an LLM agent with a numerical environment. The environment provides tools for analyzing past evaluations and executing numerical methods, while maintaining a shared evaluation history and method-specific state to support continuation across method switches. Using observations and tool feedback, the LLM agent selects tools, configures their parameters, and allocates the evaluation budget, while numerical methods compute and evaluate candidate points. Building on this system, we also introduce NextEval Bench, a benchmark protocol for comparing agent configurations on shared DFO tasks using the same numerical tools under matched evaluation budgets and information constraints. Numerical results on low-dimensional DFO problems demonstrate that the NextEval solver outperforms the state-of-the-art DFO baselines in function-evaluation efficiency.

Optimization and Control.title: Hybridizing 0/1 Knapsack and Priority-Aware TSP for Vehicle Routing: an Applied Variant of the TSP with Profits
Optimization and Control.summary: Distribution logistics with capacity constraints and service priorities can be modeled as a variant of the \emph{TSP with Profits} (TSPP), in which not all customers need to be visited and the selection of which customers to serve is part of the problem. This paper proposes an applied variant with two adaptations: (i) a 0/1 Knapsack objective function weighted by client priority squared ($v_i \cdot p_i^2$), and (ii) a priority bias in the Nearest Neighbor heuristic for the TSP, parameterized by $α$. The approach is evaluated on a scenario with 14 customers and a 1,100~kg capacity, complemented by a comparative experimental protocol against the classical greedy heuristic ($v_i/w_i$ ordering) and an integer programming solver. Results on the base scenario show 9 customers served, 96.4\% capacity utilization, and R\$~18,392.60 revenue, with all 5 excluded customers being low-priority. A sensitivity analysis of the priority exponent justifies the quadratic choice. The limitations of the hierarchical decomposition are explicitly discussed.

Optimization and Control.title: Detailed balance and phase transition in Nash equilibria of mean-field Ising game
Optimization and Control.summary: We study a finite-state mean-field game with entropic control cost. In the large population limit, we show that its stationary Nash equilibria satisfy the detailed balance condition and their distributions take the Gibbsian form with the value function playing the role of a Hamiltonian. We apply the entropic control cost to a ferromagnetic mean-field Ising game and investigate its stationary and non-stationary Nash equilibria. We find that the stationary Nash equilibria exhibit a second-order phase transition from disordered to ordered equilibria as temperature decreases. A center-manifold reduction yields non-stationary Nash equilibrium near the critical temperature and reveals the critical slowing down in the relaxation toward the stationary Nash equilibrium.

Optimization and Control.title: Learning Sequential Decisions from Multiple Sources via Group-Robust Markov Decision Processes
Optimization and Control.summary: Learning a common policy from multiple source environments requires accounting for cross-source heterogeneity, and the offline setting introduces an additional challenge of limited data coverage. We formulate this problem as a distributionally robust Markov decision process under a shared linear MDP representation with source-specific transition and reward components. The uncertainty set is constructed through feature-wise mixtures of these components, yielding a $d$-rectangular structure that captures cross-source heterogeneity and admits a robust Bellman recursion. Building on this formulation, we develop Group-Robust Pessimistic Value Iteration (GR-PEVI), an offline policy-learning algorithm that combines feature-wise worst-case aggregation with a data-dependent pessimism penalty. Under a robust partial coverage condition, we establish finite-sample suboptimality guarantees for GR-PEVI and extend the analysis to clustered sources, characterizing the trade-off between the statistical gain from pooling similar sources and the approximation error induced by within-cluster heterogeneity. Simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of GR-PEVI, with empirical behavior consistent with the theoretical analysis. We apply GR-PEVI to a multi-source electronic health record study of multiple sclerosis treatment decisions to illustrate its use in a clinical setting.

Optimization and Control.title: Linear Programming Upper Bounds for the Coil-in-the-Box Problem
Optimization and Control.summary: Let $S_n$ denote the maximum length of a coil in the $n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_n$, i.e., a simple cycle whose induced subgraph has no additional chords. We combine classical square-counting identities and structural properties of maximum coils with new valid combinatorial inequalities into a parameterized linear program whose optimal value provides an upper bound for $S_n$. For $n\ge13$, we construct two analytic dual feasible solutions. Their objective values yield upper bounds on $S_n$, and the smaller value is the exact optimum of the parameterized LP. One dual solution results in the bound \[ S_n\le 2^{n-1} \frac{8n(n-1)(5n-14)} {40n^3-131n^2+4n+136-(5n-14)\lfloor3n/4\rfloor}, \] which improves upon the upper bounds in Lukito, Lukito-van Zanten, and Zémor for $13\le n\le19853$. The second yields the upper bound \[ S_n\le 2^{n-1}\left( 1-\frac1{30\sqrt{3n}}+O(n^{-1}) \right), \] improving upon the asymptotic upper bound of Zémor. Taken together, the two bounds improve upon the upper bounds for $S_n$ in Lukito, Lukito-van Zanten, and Zémor for every $n\ge13$.

Optimization and Control.title: NAG-GS: A Semi-Implicit Stochastic Optimizer with Large-Step Stability
Optimization and Control.summary: Stochastic first-order methods are widely used for large-scale optimization and machine learning, where their performance often depends on the learning rate. We study NAG-GS, a stochastic momentum method based on a semi-implicit Gauss--Seidel discretization of a Nesterov-type flow. For strongly convex quadratics, we determine the exact range of stable step sizes for fixed damping and the step size that minimizes the worst-case spectral radius. When the damping equals the strong-convexity parameter, the method recovers the accelerated asymptotic factor $(\sqrtκ-1)/(\sqrtκ+1)$, where $κ$ is the condition number. We also prove that the quadratic iteration converges linearly with dynamic damping when its limiting fixed-damping iteration is stable. For general strongly convex, possibly nonsmooth objectives, we establish an $O(1/k)$ bound on the expected objective gap of the last iterate, using a conditionally unbiased stochastic first-order oracle with bounded second moment. The result holds with dynamic damping from any $γ_0>0$. We show that NAG-GS can also be written as a Heavy-Ball iteration with explicitly determined step sizes and momentum coefficients. We test the stochastic result on nonsmooth hinge-loss classification problems, and further evaluate NAG-GS on quadratic problems, logistic regression, convolutional neural networks, RoBERTa, and Vision Transformers. The experiments show that NAG-GS can remain effective at learning rates where standard optimizers become unstable or lose accuracy.
Optimization and Control.comment: 30 pages, 13 figures. Revised title and exposition; stochastic convergence with dynamic damping, Heavy-Ball equivalence, and nonsmooth numerical experiments

Optimization and Control.title: Boxing Problem
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the \textit{Boxing Problem}, which seeks a subset of points in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) maximizing the total reward of a selection of points minus the width of its axis-aligned bounding box. We also investigate the associated \textit{Boxing Set}, defined by the epigraph of the width function over binary selection variables. Although the width function is not submodular in general, we restore submodularity by fixing an anchor point. After anchoring, we establish a connection to the intersection of mixing sets with a linking constraint, which yields a polynomial-time optimization algorithm and a polynomial-size extended formulation. We then study the polyhedral structure of the Boxing Set and show that its facets admit laminar families of tight sets and can be obtained by sequential lifting. For the one-dimensional case, we provide a complete description of facet-defining inequalities together with a strongly polynomial-time separation algorithm.

Optimization and Control.title: Neural Compression of Long ADMM Trajectory for Multiparametric Quadratic Program
Optimization and Control.summary: Solving large-scale multiparametric quadratic programs (mpQPs) in real time often requires thousands of iterative optimization updates, creating a major computational bottleneck in model predictive control and learning-enabled systems. This paper proposes TQPNet, a self-supervised neural compression framework that learns to compress long ADMM optimization trajectories into a compact neural warm start followed by a few refinement iterations. We derive a low-dimensional ADMM scheme operating on the primal-dual variables $(x,β)$ and show that its iteration admits an equivalent ReLU-layer representation, termed ADMM(ReLU). Building on this insight, TQPNet combines a multilayer perceptron with ReLU activations (MLP(ReLU)) and a small number of unrolled ADMM(ReLU) refinement layers. The network is trained offline using an optimality-condition-informed residual loss, eliminating the need for solver-generated labels. The proposed residual-based framework enables both self-supervised training and online solution certification through adaptive ADMM(ReLU) refinement. Experiments on large-scale mpQPs and real-time MPC applications demonstrate that TQPNet achieves high accuracy, strong generalization, and substantially faster inference than conventional optimization-based methods.

Optimization and Control.title: Conformal Predictive Distributions for Contextual Order Fulfillment Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: Ship-to-home fulfillment requires a retailer to select a fulfillment location and carrier before the delivery time is known. These decisions often rely on static transit-time estimates, which cannot represent how delivery-time uncertainty varies across orders and fulfillment options. This paper constructs conformal predictive distributions (CPDs) using Conformal Predictive Systems (CPS) for regression and the cross Venn-Abers predictor (CVAP) for multiclass classification, and uses them in a contextual optimization model for fulfillment decisions. The model is solved by contextual sample-average approximation (C-SAA). The regret of each fulfillment decision, its expected cost above that of the best decision, is bounded by forecast error, scenario-evaluation error, and the candidate-generation gap. The forecast term depends on how well calibration residuals or class probabilities represent the current order. On more than five million proprietary order records, CVAP raises exact-day accuracy from 49.5% for the rule-based estimate to 64.1%. Paired with a decision rule that selects a quantile weighting late errors more heavily, the split CPS (SCPS) gives a point estimate that raises late-delivery detection from 3.8% to 79.4%. Residual-based CPS distributions also meet or slightly exceed nominal interval-coverage targets. In decision experiments with a JD.com simulator over six test dates, C-SAA with CVAP lowers mean total cost by 7.1% and C-SAA with the Mondrian CPS (MCPS) lowers it by 6.7%, relative to C-SAA with the original nonconformal forecast. Both cut the late-delivery rate from 5.7% to below 4.0%.

Optimization and Control.title: Trajectory-Planning Attitude Control System for Satellites with Magnetic Attitude Control and One Reaction Wheel
Optimization and Control.summary: Selecting attitude actuators for spacecraft in low earth orbit (LEO) often involves a trade between reaction wheels and magnetorquers. Reaction wheels generally have higher size, weight and power as well as cost, compared with magnetorquers, but have performance advantages. We consider a hybrid system relying on a single reaction wheel and three magnetorquers, using a trajectory planning control method that focuses on meeting pointing goals and minimizing the need to desaturate the reaction wheel. The use of planning allows for intelligent use of the reaction wheel and accommodates time-changing goals and orbit-varying magnetic fields. Preliminary results show trajectories with fractional-degree-accuracy, as well as management of reaction wheel momentum and avoidance of stiction. We also compare to a magnetorquer-only planning-based control system and show better convergence and faster slews.
Optimization and Control.comment: 19 pages, 26 figures in 14 groups, AAS/AIAA Astrodynamics Specialist Conference

Optimization and Control.title: Data-driven Wasserstein distributionally robust generalized Nash equilibrium problems with heterogeneous uncertainty
Optimization and Control.summary: We study stochastic generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems with heterogeneous, stochastic uncertainty in the cost functions. To address the distributional uncertainty, we let each agent construct an individual Wasserstein ambiguity set around an empirical distribution obtained from private data. We establish finite-sample robustness guarantees for any distributionally robust (DR) GNE. Focusing on variational equilibria, we derive a DR variational inequality (VI) reformulation and establish asymptotic consistency with the nominal stochastic game. Under mild conditions, we derive an exact finite-dimensional generalized Nash equilibrium reformulation. We then quantify how heterogeneous worst-case distributions affect monotonicity, and derive conditions for uniqueness and equilibrium sensitivity. To compute a variational DR GNE, we propose an inexact projected method and establish convergence under vanishing oracle errors, an asymptotic error bound under bounded oracle errors, and linear convergence under exact oracle evaluations.

Optimization and Control.title: Inexact PDHG for Large-Scale Semidefinite Programming
Optimization and Control.summary: First-order methods, such as the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method, have recently been explored for large-scale semidefinite programming (SDP). However, exact projections can be computationally prohibitive, motivating inexact projections using conditional gradient methods. Although computationally cheap and projection-free, these methods typically converge sublinearly. Recent variants, such as Spectrahedron Frank-Wolfe (Garber, 2026), achieve linear convergence in expectation near the optimal face of the spectrahedron. We develop an inexact PDHG framework with tractable spectrahedral projections using two techniques: (i) adaptive error tolerances that avoid unnecessary inner iterations while guaranteeing convergence, and (ii) a heuristic spectral warm start based on the Lanczos algorithm that accelerates Spectrahedron Frank-Wolfe by initializing near the optimal face. We establish an O(1/t) convergence rate for PDHG in the presence of projection errors and estimate the total number of inner iterations required for convergence. Experiments on large-scale SDP instances demonstrate that combining spectral warm starts with Spectrahedron Frank-Wolfe outperforms Lanczos-based inexact projections.

Optimization and Control.title: GPU-Accelerated Bregman Douglas-Rachford Splitting for Discrete Optimal Transport
Optimization and Control.summary: We present GPU-accelerated Bregman Douglas--Rachford splitting algorithm (BDRS) for discrete optimal transport problem in three input formats: an explicit cost matrix, a point cloud with a ground cost between them, and a separable cost on a regular grid. For each input format, we propose hardware-aware designs of mathematically equivalent representations for the BDRS iterations to enhance numerical stability and empirical runtime. We benchmark the three proposed implementations against eight GPU baseline solvers from the literature on the same device. We demonstrate that our implementations of BDRS achieve state-of-the-art performance on their respective input formats. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first cross-solver study of GPU DOT solvers with a unified measure of optimality.
Optimization and Control.comment: 44 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to Mathematical Programming Computation

Optimization and Control.title: SAG-Sep: Sparse Augmented Graphs and Onion-Guided Search for Rounded Capacity Cut Separation
Optimization and Control.summary: Rounded capacity cuts (RCCs) are among the most effective cuts for capacitated vehicle-routing relaxations, but exact separation is computationally prohibitive at scale. Existing heuristic and neural separators can be fast, but often fail to produce sufficiently many effective cuts within practical separation budgets. We introduce SAG-Sep, a separator that scores node membership in RCC-inducing subsets across vehicle-count levels from a fractional LP solution in a single encoder forward pass, avoiding the iterative predict-and-coarsen inference used by NeuralSEP-style separators. SAG-Sep encodes the LP solution as a Sparse Augmented Graph (SAG), adding flow-informed multi-hop edges that expose long-range routing structure without densifying attention. Beyond LP-aware sparse encoding, we observe that high-value exact RCCs are typically nested, organizing into onion-like subset families, and SAG-Sep's node scores track subset nesting depth. This motivates Onion-Sweep (OS), a training-free decoder that ranks customers by their scores, evaluates the RCC violation of every prefix of the ranking in one vectorized pass, and emits the most violated prefix of each replica together with a cross-replica family of nested proposals, converting independent node scores into structurally coordinated RCC candidates without a tuned threshold or probing band. On the NeuralSEP benchmark with N=1000 customer instances, SAG-Sep with OS reduces the average root gap by 17.7% relative to the strongest NeuralSEP baseline, while the single-pass SAG-Sep separator achieves a roughly 30-fold per-iteration neural separation speedup. Our findings suggest that LP-aware sparse encoding and the nested structure of high-value cuts are structural patterns worth leveraging in neural separation more broadly.
Optimization and Control.comment: 42 pages, 4 figures, 26 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track). Code: https://github.com/henryleo180/SAG-Sep

Optimization and Control.title: A Stochastic LineseArch Method (SLAM) for Minimizing Expectation Residuals: Weakening Boundedness of Gradient
Optimization and Control.summary: We establish convergence guarantees for the Stochastic LineseArch Method (SLAM) proposed and analyzed in Wang et al. (arXiv:2512.14979) for nonconvex composite stochastic optimization, retaining the iteration and sample complexity orders of the original analysis assuming neither the boundedness of true gradients nor the Lipschitz continuity of the convex nonsmooth term $r$. ChatGPT was used to assist in developing a key intermediate result. Under uniformly Lipschitz continuous and unbiased sampled gradients with uniformly bounded variance with mini-batch sizes proportional to the iteration budget, SLAM achieves an iteration complexity $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ and a sample complexity $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-4})$ for obtaining an iterate whose expected proximal-gradient residual norm is at most $ε$.

Optimization and Control.title: Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Online Learning
Optimization and Control.summary: We study online Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization (DRO), where the ambiguity set is a Wasserstein ball centered at the empirical distribution and evolves with each observation. We formulate each round as a zero-sum game and develop an online distributional best-response algorithm that requires only one projected subgradient step per iteration. Combining regret analysis with measure concentration, we establish explicit, instance-dependent, and high-probability convergence rates to the optimal offline DRO value.

Optimization and Control.title: Hierarchical Laminates Cannot Reproduce All Effective Properties of Planar Two-Phase Composites: A Counterexample with a 16-Component Potential
Optimization and Control.summary: Designing a composite requires understanding which effective properties can be achieved through varying its microstructure, i.e., the spatial arrangement of given constituent materials. Hierarchical laminates, created by successive layering, reach many known limits on these properties, making it natural to ask whether they can reproduce every effective response obtainable from the same constituents. We answer this question negatively for planar two-phase composites governed by linear systems whose potentials have 16 or more components. We construct constituent material properties and, at any prescribed nontrivial phase fraction, periodic microstructures whose effective properties cannot be approximated by hierarchical laminates, even when layer directions, proportions, and the number of layering steps are unrestricted. We design the constituents so that all hierarchical laminates have equal effective energies at two prescribed mean gradients. The key step is to construct a medium whose local properties are those of horizontal laminates with smoothly varying phase fractions, but whose effective energies violate this equality. Approximating these energies with sufficiently fine periodic stripes of the original constituents yields the two-phase counterexample. This construction also gives a negative answer to the two-well relaxation problem: the minimum of two positive-definite homogeneous quadratic forms on $\mathbb{R}^{2\times32}$ can have distinct quasiconvex and rank-one convex envelopes. The counterexample and the strict inequality between the envelopes are formally verified in Lean 4.
Optimization and Control.comment: 32 pages, 4 figures. Main results formally verified in Lean 4

Optimization and Control.title: Optimality of Threshold Policies for Heat Storage Optimization and a Policy Gradient Algorithm
Optimization and Control.summary:
We study the optimal control of a stylized finite-horizon heat-storage system operated by a prosumer who can buy heat from and sell heat to a district heating network. Heat production and consumption are uncertain, and charging and discharging decisions have to be taken before the subsequent heat balance is observed. The resulting problem is formulated as a Markov decision process with continuous state and action spaces. We first establish a structural characterization of the optimal policy as a two-parameter threshold policy. Under additional regularity assumptions, we prove differentiability and Lipschitz properties of the value functions.
  Exploiting the threshold structure, we parameterize the policy by the time-dependent lower and upper thresholds and derive a pathwise stochastic-gradient estimator. We then propose a projected stochastic policy-gradient algorithm, establish a constrained Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz inequality and derive global finite-sample bounds for both the objective optimality gap and the distance to the optimal threshold vector. Finally, numerical experiments for a non-stationary heat-balance process illustrate the evolution of the threshold parameters.

Optimization and Control.title: Flow Matching for Fluctuation-Based Fluorescence Super-Resolution
Optimization and Control.summary: Fluctuation-based super-resolution techniques are an appealing alternative to single-molecule and structured-illumination microscopy, as they adapt to standard acquisition settings and exploit the independent stochastic fluctuations of fluorophores across a sequence of frames. However, most existing approaches lack an explicit model of the acquisition process and provide only relative intensity estimates, limiting quantitative analyses. In this work, we combine model-based and generative approaches to exploit the full stochastic information in the sequence, proposing a reconstruction framework built on flow matching and a double-Poisson forward model accounting for blinking, blur, under-sampling and noise. The method alternates two steps: a flow matching model first learns the distribution of the acquired data; then, the sample and the background are jointly estimated by minimising a Kullback-Leibler divergence between observed and simulated distributions via regularised proximal gradient steps. On simulated and real Argolight data, the method resolves lines separated by 120 nm, outperforming SACD and eSRRF.
Optimization and Control.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, submitted to ISBI 2027. Code available at https://github.com/cozzalberto/flow_fluo

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Approximate Envy-Freeness and Pareto Optimality Beyond Additivity
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the compatibility of envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) and Pareto optimality (PO) beyond additive valuations. For two agents with monotone submodular valuations, we prove that a $2/3$-EF1+PO allocation always exists, while for every $α>3/4$, an $α$-EF1+PO allocation may fail to exist even for unweighted coverage valuations. A six-good EF1+PO counterexample resolves the longstanding exact existence question negatively.
  Exact EF1+PO does exist when one agent has a monotone submodular valuation and the remaining agents have identical additive valuations. For two agents, we also establish tight EF$k$+PO item thresholds of $4k+1$, $2k+1$, and $3k+1$ for two submodular agents, two subadditive agents, and one subadditive and one additive agent, respectively. Finally, deciding whether an EF$k$+PO allocation exists is NP-hard for every fixed integer $k\ge1$, even for three agents with unweighted coverage valuations, one of whom has an additive valuation.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 25 pages, which includes three appendices

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Strategyproof Deep Reinforcement Learning for Online Resource Allocation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Online resource allocation faces two coupled challenges: (1) allocating scarce resources efficiently under uncertain future demand, and (2) ensuring that agents report task valuations and requirements truthfully (strategyproofness). Reinforcement Learning (RL) adapts allocation decisions through experience but does not necessarily ensure strategyproofness. Existing strategyproof RL uses a linear allocation rule, which limits the resource interactions it can represent. Neural mechanism design methods offer greater expressiveness, but provide only approximate incentive guarantees. Against this background, we introduce the first strategyproof deep RL mechanism for online resource allocation. It integrates three novel components: (i) a monotonic neural network that learns nonlinear interactions by construction (higher reported value cannot reduce acceptance, while a longer reported duration or larger resource requirement cannot increase it); (ii) a generalised critical payment: the lowest accepted value, with all other inputs fixed; and (iii) training by either RL or imitation of an existing rule. Together, monotonicity and the critical payment ensure strategyproofness and individual rationality, while the neural rule provides flexibility and imitation improves training efficiency. Empirically, on a four-resource stream with two partner pairs that a linear difference cannot represent, the neural rule achieves 97.8% of an offline welfare upper bound, compared with 93.8% for a linear learner and 89.0% for first-come, first-served, closing 65% and 80% of the remaining optimality gap, respectively. Moreover, imitation reaches 97.5% in only 261 seconds, about 89 times faster than RL.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 15 pages, 2 figures

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Game-Theoretic Solvers with Bayesian Opponent Modeling and Moral Rhetoric Framing for GLEE
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We describe the agent we submitted to the GLEE Competition, which plays bargaining, negotiation, and persuasion games against a shared pool of human and AI opponents. The agent is built around three central components: a classical game-theoretic solver to compute numeric moves, an online Bayesian layer to estimate opponent archetypes, and a language model to write accompanying messages. We utilize Rubinstein bargaining for bargaining, Faratin concession for negotiation, and Kamenica--Gentzkow disclosure for persuasion, and adapt those models to live opponents using two separate layers: a Bayesian estimate of the opponent's hidden discount factor, reservation value, or signaling reliability, and a Thompson sampling bandit over five moral-foundation framings coupled with an evidence-intuition spectrum to establish message register. Most of the development effort went into the recurring problem that theoretically optimal policies perform poorly in certain live settings; we report associated failure modes, guardrails we built, and our hypotheses. We additionally evaluate our model over 13,200 Monte Carlo games against 11 synthetic opponent archetypes, an ablation of the opponent-modeling layer, and an extensive analysis of 9,337 live-game messages in which moral rhetoric framing in the persuasion setting is strongly correlated with whether the buyer purchased ($χ^2=616.7$, $p \approx 3.7\times10^{-132}$), surviving controls for quality, round, and configuration.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 13 pages, 1 figure; accepted to 1st Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB) @ NeurIPS 2026

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Nash Incentive-compatible Online Mechanism Learning via Weakly Differentially Private Online Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study a multi-round mechanism design problem, where we interact with a set of agents over a sequence of rounds. We wish to design an incentive-compatible (IC) online learning scheme to maximize an application-specific objective within a given class of mechanisms, without prior knowledge of the agents' type distributions. Even if each mechanism in this class is IC in a single round, if an algorithm naively chooses from this class on each round, the entire learning process may not be IC against non-myopic buyers who appear over multiple rounds. On each round, our method randomly chooses between the recommendation of a weakly differentially private online learning algorithm (e.g., Hedge), and a commitment mechanism which penalizes non-truthful behavior. Our method is IC and achieves $O(T^{\frac{1+h}{2}})$ regret for the application-specific objective in an adversarial setting, where $h$ quantifies the long-sightedness of the agents. When compared to prior work, our approach is conceptually simpler,it applies to general mechanism design problems (beyond auctions), and its regret scales gracefully with the size of the mechanism class.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: ICML 2024, 18 pages. v2 corrects minor errors in the published version

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Conservative Policy Iteration For Zero-Sum POSGs
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Occupancy-state reductions make dynamic programming possible for zero-sum partially observable stochastic games (zs-POSGs). Existing point-based solvers usually optimise a central value function. This restores Bellman recursion, but it requires point-based updates over high-dimensional occupancy spaces. We introduce an approximate policy-iteration algorithm for finite-horizon zs-POSGs. The method maintains one policy per player and updates both jointly along occupancy trajectories induced by conservative policy updates. Instead of approximating a full central value function, each update uses a single supporting hyperplane induced by the current joint policy. The algorithm alternates local policy improvements, conservative updates, and persistent exploration. Computation is therefore concentrated on occupancy regions where the current joint policy is exploitable. On finite-horizon zero-sum POSG benchmarks, the method is competitive at small horizons and often improves the runtime-exploitability trade-off at larger horizons compared with PBVI, HSVI, and CFR+.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Optimal Auction Design for Constrained Buyers
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study single-parameter, multi-buyer auctions in which buyers are subject to constraints that affect their bidding strategy. Such constraints arise in many real-world auction settings and fundamentally alter the auction design space: the revelation principle, envelope theorem, and Myerson's lemma no longer hold. Our focus is on a large family of constraints where the buyers do not have a hard budget-cap, but are restricted in how they can bid or spend their budget --- including no-overbidding, ex-post individual rationality (IR), and stagewise IR. We ask whether the seller can leverage the buyers' constraints to obtain improved payoff.
  We separate between \emph{revenue-aligned} seller objectives (revenue, welfare, or any linear combination), and \emph{consumer-aligned} seller objectives (e.g.\ consumer surplus). For the former, we establish a unified theory for all constraints in the family, which parallels Myerson's theory of optimal auctions for unconstrained buyers. We develop a new measure-theoretic technique to show that Myerson-style auctions remain optimal, despite the altered design space and failure of the classical theory's central tenets. In contrast, we show a consumer-aligned seller can leverage the buyers' strategic limitations to strictly outperform mechanisms that are classically incentive compatible. We also design an auction arbitrarily close to optimal for buyers who cannot tolerate temporary debt.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: When do token systems stabilize? Compatibility constraints and community structure
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Token systems support repeated service exchange without monetary transfers, but their viability depends on the stability of token balances. We study token systems with compatibility constraints among agents. A requester is randomly sampled in each period, and only a few randomly sampled agents are available to provide service. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for stability and show that the minimum-token rule, which selects the available provider with the lowest token balance, achieves the optimal stability region. We then apply this stability criterion to a random token system generated from stochastic block models with uniformly sampled requesters. We tightly characterize the stability regime by identifying two obstructions to stability: insufficient service opportunities for a group of communities or for an individual agent.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Rethinking Data Value: Asymmetric Data Shapley for Structure-Aware Valuation in AI Model Markets
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Modern AI model markets assemble models from heterogeneous pipeline contributions, including raw data, derivative data, and data-related services, whose value can depend on upstream inputs and inherited model states. Conventional valuation approaches focus on data contributions without explicitly accounting for these production relationships. They can therefore misattribute value by evaluating contributions outside their upstream production context. We formalize this pipeline-context valuation mismatch and develop Asymmetric Data Shapley (ADS), a unified framework for structure-aware value attribution. ADS translates documented production relationships into ordered valuation groups and evaluates contributions among peers conditional on their upstream production context. We provide an axiomatic characterization of the resulting allocation and quantify allocation uncertainty when evidence supports multiple valuation structures. To support valuation at larger scales or with costly utility evaluations, we develop a Monte Carlo estimator (MC-ADS) and a surrogate-assisted estimator (SA-MC-ADS). Experiments show that ignoring production dependencies systematically shifts value toward redundant derivative data and away from useful upstream data and services. Moreover, experiments on derivative data selection and on dataset procurement during multi-stage large language model fine-tuning show that decisions guided by ADS improve downstream model performance relative to the respective benchmarks.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Substantially revised and expanded: updated title and abstract, extended theoretical analysis of ADS and uncertain pipeline structure, surrogate-assisted estimation, and revised experiments

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Characterizing Maximum Nash Welfare: Envy-Freeness and Proportionality
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: When allocating indivisible goods, the maximum Nash welfare rule is known to be the unique welfarist rule satisfying envy-freeness up to one good. We strengthen this characterization by showing that envy-freeness up to one good can be replaced by substantially weaker fairness requirements: envy-freeness up to $k$ goods or proportionality up to $k$ goods, for any fixed $k$. Our characterization holds even for profiles with identical goods.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Impossibility of No-Regret in Multi-Agent Bidding
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We consider $T$ repeated second-price auctions across $n$ pacing bidders with i.i.d. item arrivals, and show that it is computationally impossible for all bidders to achieve no-regret simultaneously while satisfying their respective budget or return-on-investment constraints. Therefore, in the prominent internet auction systems where buyers simultaneously deploy pacing algorithms or automated bidding agents, we cannot hope to achieve joint no-regret guarantees in general.
  We establish a deterministic relationship that high variance in online bidding systems implies high regret. By showing that one can extract a pacing equilibrium from a low-variance system, we prove PPAD-hardness of attaining joint no-regret. For several widely used bidding algorithms, we also show evidence from dynamical systems and numerical simulations that they can indeed display high-variance behavior through cycling, even on simple market instances.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: PDE-Based Bounds on Optimal Exponents in Active Simple Hypothesis Testing
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We present general upper and lower bounds on the optimal error exponent for the Active Simple Hypothesis Testing (ASHT) problem. ASHT has been extensively studied across diverse fields including Information Theory, Bandits, and Operations Research, a precise characterization of this optimal exponent has remained elusive. This work combines a recent Partial Differential Equation (PDE) characterization of the optimal exponent by Vijayan (2025) with the comparison principle of viscosity solutions of Hamilton-Jacobi PDEs. This leads to bounds that are parametrized by convex functions, sets and lower Hamiltonian relaxations, a flexibility that generalizes many known results in the literature.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Tight Characterizations of AMM Mechanism Design under Weak Efficiency
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Miner extractable value (MEV) poses a persistent challenge for blockchain ecosystems. It arises from the fact that a block builder can exploit its unilateral control over transaction inclusion and ordering to extract profit, potentially at users' expense. Recent work has explored consensus-aided mechanism design to mitigate MEV. This approach combines generic consensus-layer guarantees with application-layer mechanisms that use these guarantees to address application-specific MEV problems.
  Prior work exemplifies this approach for automated market makers (AMMs). When the consensus layer offers fair sequencing, which orders transactions according to their arrival times, their proposed mechanism achieves incentive compatibility (IC) and weak local efficiency (wLE). Informally, IC rules out profitable strategic deviations by users and builders. Meanwhile, wLE ensures that after execution, any order willing to trade at the initial price cannot benefit from further trade with the pool at the ending marginal price.
  In this work, we resolve the main open question left by prior works: whether IC and wLE can be achieved under plain consensus (e.g., current Ethereum) without fair sequencing. We prove that no deterministic, anonymous batch AMM can achieve both properties. The impossibility holds even when the consensus layer guarantees censorship resilience and block space is unlimited, establishing the first separation between censorship resilience and fair sequencing in the context of decentralized mechanism design.
  Our impossibility proof combines three strategic capabilities: creating Sybil identities, over-reporting budgets, and misreporting values. We further show the tightness of our impossibility result: removing any one from the strategy space restores feasibility under censorship resilience. Specifically, we construct a mechanism achieving IC and wLE for each restricted setting.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Abstract shortened to comply with arXiv's character limit

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Sybil-Proofness of Generalized Adaptive Clinching and Implications for Blockchain Mechanism Design
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
The adaptive clinching auction of Dobzinski, Lavi, and Nisan (FOCS'08) is a cornerstone of mechanism design with budget-constrained bidders, and it has since inspired a broad range of extensions to substantially richer market settings. Adaptive clinching enjoys compelling guarantees: it is Pareto optimal, and truthful bidding is a dominant strategy whenever budgets cannot be overreported. In many real-world environments, however, identities are cheap to create, making resilience to Sybil attacks an additional requirement. Whether the guarantees of adaptive clinching survive when a bidder can split its budget across fake identities has remained open. We introduce a generalized framework for adaptive clinching and prove that it satisfies Sybil-robust incentive compatibility: a bidder cannot benefit from splitting into any finite number of identities with arbitrary value reports, provided their aggregate reported budget does not exceed the bidder's enforceable true budget. Sybil resilience thus joins the list of ideal properties of adaptive clinching.
  Our work is motivated by practical problems in decentralized finance, where automated market makers (AMMs) are among the most widely used applications. We design a new AMM mechanism that extends classical adaptive clinching in two ways: it supports a two-sided market and protects against two-sided strategies, and it allows the supply function to depend on the auction state. Its one-sided special case is captured by our generalized adaptive clinching framework, and our proof techniques show that the full two-sided mechanism simultaneously satisfies Sybil-robust incentive compatibility and a relaxed notion of Pareto optimality. We argue that these guarantees are essentially the best possible via impossibility results. More broadly, our work reveals new connections between classical algorithmic game theory and modern decentralized blockchains.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Abstract shortened to comply with arXiv's character limit

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Noise Shapes the Surplus: Strategic Play Against No-Regret Learners
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Recent work has shown that, in zero-sum games, an optimizer can extract $Ω(\sqrt{T})$ strategic surplus---cumulative payoff above the minimax benchmark---against noiseless no-regret learners with a constant step size. However, in practice, learners often act on perturbed payoff scores and use decaying learning rates $η_t$. Since existing extraction mechanisms rely on exact scores, a natural question is whether noise shields the learner from exploitation and eliminates surplus altogether.
  We address this question for the widely used class of Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL) algorithms. Under standard regularity conditions, we establish three results, none of which assumes independence of the noise. First, under summability conditions, passive play of a strategy fixed independently of the horizon earns at most constant surplus.
