These findings indicate that users' evacuation behavior is shaped not only by the environment itself but also by the collective behavior of surrounding agents, underscoring the need to consider how agent behavior affects users' psychological states during training.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: The 2nd International Workshop on Trust and Blame in Multi-Person Multi-Agent Societies (TBSA_2nd) in conjunction with HAI 2026, 7 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Generative AI as a Mediator in Creator Collaboration: Challenges, Design Opportunities, and Concerns
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: As Generative AI (GenAI) expands beyond individual workflows and becomes increasingly integrated intocollaborative creative work, its potential to address the fundamental challenge of building common groundamong creators with diverse expertise remains underexplored. Specifically, we lack empirical understandingof how GenAI can mediate collaboration asymmetries among heterogeneous creators. To address this gap,we conducted a multi-method study with narrative writers (N = 10) and visual designers (N = 10) in thecontext of game development. Our findings demonstrate that GenAI goes beyond individual assistance toserve as a collaborative mediator by aligning creative intent, sustaining shared understanding, and mitigatinginterpersonal friction among creators. At the same time, we highlight concerns that GenAI may reducecommunication among creators, undermine mutual trust, and reshape interpersonal dynamics and collaborativeprocesses. Based on these insights, we identify design opportunities for GenAI tools that nurture collaborativesynergy while preserving the creativity and values of human work.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 37 pages. Published in Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (PACMHCI), CSCW 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: StreamStudio: Exploring Video Authoring with Streaming Autoregressive Generation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We present StreamStudio, a prototype system that explores a new authoring paradigm for streaming video generation. Instead of entering a prompt and waiting for a complete video before making changes, creators can interact with the generation as it unfolds: steering what comes next, returning to earlier moments, and exploring different continuations. In this way, StreamStudio shifts creative control from post-generation revision to continuous interaction with the generative process. Our contribution centers on this authoring paradigm and the interaction mechanisms that make streaming generation directly manipulable. StreamStudio is designed as a plug-and-play interface that can work with compatible generation and editing models, allowing its interaction model to evolve alongside advances in underlying video models. As streaming models become faster and easier to control in the future, such an interface may support more flexible and controllable video creation, including richer edits and multimodal interventions during generation.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: PRISM: Festina Lente Proactivity -- Risk-Sensitive, Uncertainty-Aware Deliberation for Proactive Agents
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Proactive agents must decide not only what to say but also whether and when to intervene. Many current systems rely on brittle heuristics or indiscriminate long reasoning, which offers little control over the benefit-burden tradeoff. We formulate the problem as cost-sensitive selective intervention and present PRISM, a novel framework that couples a decision-theoretic gate with a dual-process reasoning architecture. At inference time, the agent intervenes only when a calibrated probability of user acceptance exceeds a threshold derived from asymmetric costs of missed help and false alarms. Inspired by festina lente (Latin: "make haste slowly"), we gate by an acceptance-calibrated, cost-derived threshold and invoke a resource-intensive Slow mode with counterfactual checks only near the decision boundary, concentrating computation on ambiguous and high-stakes cases. Training uses gate-aligned, schema-locked distillation: a teacher running the full PRISM pipeline provides dense, executable supervision on unlabeled interaction traces, while the student learns a response policy that is explicitly decoupled from the intervention gate to enable tunable and auditable control. On ProactiveBench, PRISM reduces false alarms by 22.78% and improves F1 by 20.14% over strong baselines. These results show that principled decision-theoretic gating, paired with selective slow reasoning and aligned distillation, yields proactive agents that are precise, computationally efficient, and controllable. To facilitate reproducibility, we release our code, models, and resources at https://prism-festinalente.github.io/; all experiments use the open-source ProactiveBench benchmark.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Arapai: An Offline-First LLM Architecture for Adaptive Learning in Low-Connectivity Environments
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Artificial intelligence and large language models (LLMs) are transforming educational technology by enabling conversational tutoring, personalised explanations, and inquiry-driven learning. However, most AI-based learning systems rely on continuous internet connectivity and cloud-based computation, limiting their use in bandwidth-constrained environments. This paper presents Arapai, an offline-first large language model architecture designed for AI-assisted learning in low-connectivity settings. The system performs all inference locally using quantized language models and incorporates hardware-aware model selection to enable deployment on low-specification, CPU-only devices. By removing dependence on cloud infrastructure, the system provides curriculum-aligned explanations and structured academic support through natural-language interaction. To support learners at different educational stages, the system includes adaptive response levels that generate explanations at varying levels of complexity: Simple English, Lower Secondary, Upper Secondary, and Technical. The system was evaluated with 120 students and 9 instructors from secondary and tertiary institutions under limited-connectivity conditions. Results indicate stable operation on legacy hardware, acceptable response times of 1-3 seconds for typical queries, and positive user perceptions of its effectiveness in supporting self-directed learning.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: The statement that "The system was evaluated with 120 students and 9 instructors from secondary and tertiary institutions" is inaccurate

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Decompose, Don't Expand: Capability-Independent AI Systems by Construction
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: A recurring design choice in building AI systems is whether, when a task is too hard for a model, to expand the model (make it larger, better-prompted, fine-tuned), or to decompose the task (extract the parts that admit a deterministic solution to a host, leaving the model only the irreducibly fuzzy residue). We make three claims. First, that many tasks commonly delegated whole to a model are in fact deterministic tasks with a small generative core. Second, and our central empirical result, that decomposing such a task yields a measurable and desirable property we call parity by construction: on the extracted sub-tasks the model-size performance curve becomes flat, because no model performs them at all. We measure this across nine models spanning a 494M-parameter local checkpoint to a frontier Opus-class model, a thirty-fold parameter range on the local family alone: once the host resolves the context, operation selection scores identically for all nine models and selector resolution for eight of nine, while the one task that does not decompose, labelling, remains sloped across the same range. Because the task leaves the model, a stock checkpoint suffices: no task-specific training and no fine-tuning. Third, that this is a general design discipline, not a domain trick: we show the same move recurring across physics setup, motion retargeting, and object-model editing, and in a Web-CLI tool family (same author, so not an independent replication). We give a method for locating the cut, the construction that makes a cut exist (a deterministic surface and a closed grammar over it), and a way to make the residue safe (resolve the deterministic context; verify the generative output), position the work against neuro-symbolic AI, tool-augmented language models, and generate-and-verify approaches, and are explicit about what is measured (one domain) versus illustrative (the rest).

Human-Computer Interaction.title: LogicTree: Object-Oriented Writing for Structured Human-AI Academic Authoring
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Academic writing is non-linear, iterative, and structure-driven, requiring authors to develop fragmented ideas into arguments with local coherence and global consistency. However, current AI-assisted tools primarily exchange linear prompts and free-form text, forcing authors to reconstruct generated logic and repeatedly verify its alignment with their structural intentions. We propose object-oriented writing (OOW), an OOD-inspired representation and interaction paradigm in which persistent writing objects serve as shared, manipulable referents for authors and AI. We instantiate OOW in LogicTree, an Overleaf-integrated prototype that combines a hierarchical object representation with a structure-grounded writing assistance module for author-initiated generation and issue-grounded revision and a structural logical review module for inspecting local coherence and global consistency. A within-subjects study (N=12) provides initial evidence that, in controlled academic writing tasks, LogicTree helps users structure ideas, reduces workload, and improves measured logical quality compared with a conversational baseline.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Beauty Is Human: When People Love AI-Generated Art, They Think a Human Made It
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI now produces images and poems that people cannot reliably distinguish from human-made work, so people often judge for themselves who made a work. We examine how these perceived-authorship judgments relate to aesthetic preference. In a public online AI Art Turing Test, 11,123 people judged whether each of 50 pictures (26 AI-generated) was made by a human and were asked for their favourite. Among the 9,152 respondents who judged their favourite, a picture was 22.1 percentage points more likely to be judged human-made when it was the respondent's favourite, holding respondent and picture fixed. The association was similar for AI-generated and human-made favourites, was positive for all 50 pictures, and appeared under every reported detection strategy. Respondents most negative about AI art chose fewer AI-generated favourites (47% against 60% among the most positive) but more often believed them human-made, partly because others also judged those pictures human. As a result, in every opinion group a third to two fifths of respondents named an AI-generated favourite they believed human-made. A reanalysis of a published experiment on AI-generated poetry, in which 230 people rated each poem before judging its authorship, found the same pattern, although the AI poems were rated higher. When provenance is hidden, liking and perceived human authorship travel together, consistent with aesthetic response serving as evidence of a human maker and with beliefs about the maker shaping enjoyment. The findings qualify research on bias against AI art, which typically uses explicit labels, and inform AI disclosure policy.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 22 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Working paper

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Introducing M: A Modular, Modifiable Social Robot
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We present M, an open-source, low-cost tabletop social robot platform aimed at lowering barriers to social robotics research by making robots easier to reproduce, modify, and deploy in real-world settings. M combines a modular mechanical design, multimodal sensing, and expressive yet mechanically simple actuation architecture with a ROS2-native software package that cleanly separates perception, expression control, and data management. The platform includes a simulation environment with interface equivalence to hardware to support easy sim-to-real transfer of interaction behaviors. We demonstrate extensibility through additional sensing/actuation modules and provide example interaction templates for storytelling and two-way conversational coaching. Lastly, we report real-world use of M in interaction design and week-long in-home deployments, showing how M can serve as a practical platform for longitudinal, reproducible social robotics research.

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: The Power Watershed as a Differentiable Segmentation Layer
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Can a Watershed transform, the classical tool of morphological segmentation, be placed at the end of a deep network and trained through? The Power Watershed (PW) is the limit of the seeded Random Walker (RW) as p grows to infinity with edge weights raised to the power p. At every finite p the RW solves a sparse positive-definite linear system and is exactly differentiable with respect to the edge weights and the unaries through one adjoint solve; its multi-label form costs one right-hand side per label, and its limit is the PW. We study this family as the last layer of a segmentation network, the watershed layer (WS layer). A conditioning study measures how the solve, the gradient and the distance to the limit evolve with p, and the implicit gradient is checked against unrolling. On synthetic data with correct edge costs the WS layer transforms a soft prediction into an exact boundary. On nuclei segmentation (PanNuke), a binary WS layer is level with a thresholded U-Net. With the instances as labels, the WS layer turns the U-Net into an instance segmenter whose number of labels is set per image by the markers rather than by the output layout, and the network is trained through that partition: instance F1 score rises from 0.656 to 0.795 over a U-Net with connected components, level with the same network followed by a tuned marker watershed. At the training temperature the partition is a watershed of the learned costs, and the finite temperature lets the solve hedge, discounting weak markers and sharing contested pixels. The hedging puts the WS layer 0.015--0.020 F1 ahead of the baseline when trained on a tenth of the data, at the price of having to deploy the finite-p solve rather than its exact limit at inference. Code and the full experimental record are released.

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Diffusion-based Evolutionary Optimization for 3D Multi-Objective Molecular Generation
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: De novo 3D molecular design with multiple properties and fragment-retention constraints is formulated as a constrained multi-objective optimization problem. Existing 3D diffusion models provide strong capabilities for generating novel molecules, but adapting them to new conditions and multi-objective optimization tasks remains difficult. We present Diffusion-based Evolutionary Molecular Optimization (DEMO), a framework that draws solely on the unconditional molecular prior of a frozen pretrained diffusion model to generate chemically valid 3D candidates, while evolutionary search handles conditional generation and constrained multi-objective optimization, without retraining or fine-tuning. DEMO performs crossover and mutation on intermediate diffusion states through an Evolutionary-Guided Diffusion (EGD) operator, combines 2D topology and 3D geometry in Structure-Aware Environmental Selection (SAES) to preserve structural diversity, and uses three cooperating populations to coordinate structural exploration, fragment-constraint satisfaction, and property optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that EGD outperforms task-specific conditional generators in property targeting; SAES preserves structural diversity while retaining competitive hypervolume in multi-objective optimization; and DEMO improves objective convergence and generates diverse feasible molecules under fragment constraints. These results show how evolutionary search can reuse existing diffusion models for diverse molecular design requirements.

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Peer-Relative Trust-Guided Update Screening for Robust Semi-Decentralized Federated Learning under Label-Flipping Attacks
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Trust and reputation mechanisms can reduce the influence of malicious clients in federated learning (FL), but strict update filtering is difficult under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data because honest local updates may temporarily reduce performance on a shared validation proxy. Extending an earlier trust-based semi-decentralized FL (SDFL) framework, this paper operationalizes the trust signals and introduces peer-relative update screening that combines a robust validation-utility score with direction- and norm-based update quality. The method is evaluated with 50 MNIST clients, 20% persistent label-flip attackers, Dirichlet heterogeneity levels of 0.5 and 0.1, 100 communication rounds, and five paired random seeds. Under moderate heterogeneity, the proposed method reaches 98.37% final accuracy while rejecting 95.82% of malicious updates and retaining 90.30% of benign updates; the final benign and malicious trust distributions are completely separated (KS=1.00). Under severe heterogeneity, it reaches 95.25% accuracy, rejects 88.55% of malicious updates, and retains 76.90% of benign updates (KS=0.96). Trust weighting alone preserves slightly higher utility in the most heterogeneous condition, but accepts all malicious submissions. The results therefore distinguish influence mitigation from explicit containment and quantify the utility-selectivity trade-off introduced by screening. The study provides an empirically validated off-chain governance core that can feed blockchain-based audit and incentive layers in SDFL.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: 9th International Conference on Blockchain Technology and Applications (ICBTA 2026)

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: FPGAFly: A 166.7k-Neuron Fruit-Fly Connectome on One FPGA via Deferred Spike Expansion and Shared-Codeword States
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Synapse-resolution fruit-fly (Drosophila) connectomes enable neuron-by-neuron simulation of entire insect nervous systems, yet whole-brain models still require computationally demanding software or multiple neuromorphic chips, and single FPGAs support only small or statistical networks. Scaling to the full connectome, per-synapse spike expansion scales queue traffic with fan-out up to 11.2k, while 41-bit neuron states require 6.83 Mbit, exceeding the 6.27 Mbit on-chip block static RAM (BSRAM) of the target device. FPGAFly runs the 166.7k-neuron, 25.6M-connection leaky integrate-and-fire male central nervous system (CNS) connectome on one FPGA. Order-preserving deferred expansion queues one 64-bit descriptor per spike in source-ID order, cutting external memory traffic by 54.5%-57.9% and peak queue data by 95.6%-96.5% with bit-identical results. A 24-bit encoding shares codewords across normal, refractory, and quantized out-of-range states, reducing BSRAM usage from 438 to 270 with 1245 extra LUTs and zero changes across 10,000 MNIST predictions. At 80 MHz on a Gowin GW5AST-LV138, each 100 ms window finishes in 86.83 ms on average and within 93.05 ms across 2000 tests, realizing the first complete Drosophila CNS connectome simulation on one FPGA.

Methodology.title: Tabular foundation models are not a shortcut to calibrated clinical risk prediction: a pre-registered simulation against the true risk
Methodology.summary: Tabular foundation models are pretrained networks that predict risk from a table without fitting a model. Whether their risks are correct (calibrated) has been judged on real data, where true risk is unknown. In a pre-registered simulation with known true risks, we compared TabPFN-3.5, TabICLv2 and Mitra-v2 with Firth logistic regression with intercept correction (FLIC) in 58 scenarios and 1,000 random designs, then on four clinical data sets. Foundation models were not a shortcut to calibration. Their calibration slope matched FLIC's within the pre-registered margin in 36 or 37 of 48 core scenarios and was better only at n = 200 with a 3% event rate. Even 3,000 patients were often not enough: with FLIC, TabPFN-3.5 or Mitra-v2, 63%-83% of samples gave risks close to the truth in average, intercept and slope at event rates of 10% and 30%, and 35%-50% at 3%. TabICLv2 did worse (8%-39% and 1%-3%). Across the random designs, foundation models had a lower true calibration error than FLIC beyond the margin in 25%-38% and a higher one in none, though small losses were predicted at n = 3000. On real data, no model resisted a change in event rate between populations; recalibration on 500 local patients largely repaired it.
Methodology.comment: 37 pages, 7 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Information (55 pages) as an ancillary file. Pre-registered on OSF Registries (doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/8HMTZ). Code: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23737378; benchmark data: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23737416

Methodology.title: Noise Calibration and Exact Recovery for Multiview Ordinal Rearrangement Data
Methodology.summary: We studied simultaneous recovery of a latent group count, subject partition, and signature means from multiview ordinal ranks. A normalized reference rearrangement score is an affine Spearman correlation; the problem concerns the information retained by several such scores and their noise geometry. We develop an ordered-gap estimator with direction-specific concentration radii. Its finite-sample guarantee separates signature noise, missing groups, and candidate coverage, and allows the group count to grow under an attainable-margin condition. A coordinatewise partition followed by label-tuple refinement recovers groups even when every individual coordinate has population collisions. A binary-code construction explains why the one-dimensional inverse-group margin restriction need not govern a retained coordinate bank. We derive actual-law concentration from bounded ranking modules and a fixed-dimensional combinatorial central limit theorem under an observed permutation representation. A binary ordinal submodel gives logarithmic exact-recovery information scales. A subject-effect construction distinguishes persistent overlap from reducible measurement noise, and an additional ordinal anchor quantifies how new information lowers that error floor. Five focused simulation scenarios illustrate direction-specific calibration, growing-group recovery, coordinate collision resolution, variance reduction, and the effect of an additional ordinal anchor.

Methodology.title: Convex Mixed-Integer Programming for Invariant Predictions from Multi-environment Data
Methodology.summary: Heterogeneous data provide an opportunity to identify causal predictors by revealing which predictive relationships remain invariant. Under a linear model, we introduce a least-squares coefficient-and-risk (LSCR) invariance principle, requiring both ordinary least squares coefficients and prediction risks to remain constant across environments. Our model neither specifies an intervention mechanism nor assumes a structural causal model for the entire system. We develop an invariance score that quantifies departures from LSCR invariance and use its optimization to construct two complementary procedures for causal predictor identification. First, we propose an estimator that jointly minimizes prediction risk and invariance penalty, and establish non-asymptotic guarantees for estimation and recovery of the causal parents under suitable identifiability conditions. Second, without requiring full identifiability, we develop a testing procedure that minimizes the invariance score over all predictor sets excluding a given variable, enabling valid causal discoveries with asymptotic error control via a multiplier bootstrap. Both procedures admit convex mixed-integer optimization formulations that avoid exhaustive subset enumeration while providing certificates of optimality. Simulations and real data experiments demonstrate substantial statistical and computational improvements over existing methods.

Methodology.title: An Analysis of High-Dimensional Land-Water Transitions in the Great Lakes via a Bayesian Discrepancy Model for Multinomial Data
Methodology.summary: Global water-level systems have undergone large changes in recent years. Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) land cover data can be used to monitor and understand these changes. However, such data are extremely high-dimensional making them difficult to process while accounting for all sources of uncertainty. Bayesian hierarchical models are commonly implemented using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods which can be computationally expensive for large datasets. Exact Posterior Regression (EPR) provides an efficient alternative for inference in latent Gaussian hierarchical models under exponential families without requiring MCMC or approximate Bayesian strategies. EPR has not been developed for multinomial data, and we extend this class of models to the multinomial setting. Additionally, we explore signal-to-noise covariance properties of discrepancy models, which we expect to be present in our data. We extend EPR to multinomial likelihoods via a stick-breaking construction to analyze water-level changes. Through simulation studies, we compare the proposed multinomial EPR approach with alternative models implemented using Gibbs sampling and the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). We evaluate each approach based on regression parameter estimation, category probability estimation, and computational efficiency. Overall, EPR and INLA achieve substantial reductions in computation time while EPR shows improved metrics in estimation and prediction.

Methodology.title: Proximal R2 Priors for Structured Variance Allocation
Methodology.summary: Scientific domain knowledge in regression often concerns structural relationships among model terms, which are typically encoded as parameter constraints. Since such relationships rarely hold exactly in practice, prior distributions should encourage them while at the same time retaining support for scientifically plausible departures. Accounting for these relationships becomes more pressing in modern regression, where high-dimensionality is usually present and regularisation is essential. $R^2$ decomposition priors provide an interpretable foundation for regularisation by placing a prior on total explained variance and distributing the implied signal across model terms. We introduce the Proximal R2 prior, which uses proximal relaxations to encode these relationships as soft constraints on the variance allocation. Our formulation yields differentiable posteriors compatible with standard gradient based samplers. Theoretically, we prove that our prior preserves the characteristic marginal properties of global-local shrinkage priors. Moreover, we establish posterior consistency and contraction rates in growing dimensions, showing that the inclusion of structural relationships and proximal methods do not alter the shrinkage properties. Notably, these results demonstrate that the structural constraints in the model do not hinder posterior recovery. Simulation studies and real-data applications to interaction and generalised additive models demonstrate that our prior improves parameter recovery, out-of-sample prediction, and sampling efficiency over existing constrained and unconstrained shrinkage priors, even under structural misspecification.

Methodology.title: Principal-agent hypothesis testing under adaptive experimentation
Methodology.summary: Principal-agent hypothesis testing studies statistical contracts in which a principal rewards an agent according to data the agent generates. Existing work focuses on the single-shot setting, where the agent produces a single dataset. We extend the framework to sequential settings, where evidence accumulates over time, rewards may be deferred to the end or disbursed incrementally, and the agent may stop the contract at a strategically chosen stopping time. We call a contract null-deterring if no ''null agent'' (those whose data-generating distribution lies in the null hypothesis) can profit in expectation under any stopping rule, and our main conceptual result shows that such contracts are characterized by e-processes. We then turn to the agent's best response and identify the optimal stopping rule through the Snell envelope of the reward process. We develop simpler, more interpretable approximations that often require the agent to have only partial knowledge of its distribution.

Methodology.title: Using Multiple Outcomes to Adjust Standard Errors for Spatial Correlation
Methodology.summary: A researcher interested in a particular outcome variable often observes dozens of other outcomes for the same units. If these auxiliary outcomes exhibit the same cross-sectional correlation as the outcome of interest, they can be used to estimate that correlation directly. We develop a procedure that uses estimates of this form to adjust standard errors in a given regression problem. We show, theoretically and with simulations, that the resulting standard errors can be substantially more accurate. Re-analyzing nine papers, we find that the proposed correction can make a meaningful difference in practice.

Methodology.title: Pinpointing Pivot Points: The DECIDE Framework for Data Analysis Decision Importances
Methodology.summary: Human judgment calls made throughout the data science life cycle can change the conclusions drawn from data. Independent analysts often make different choices when given the same data, leading to often unacceptable variations in results and contributing to the ongoing reproducibility crisis across scientific disciplines. The rapid adoption of agentic tools threatens to amplify this crisis. Several approaches have been developed to address this variation by following the same strategy: repeating an analysis under different combinations of analytical decisions and inspecting the distribution of outcomes. Examples include multiverse analysis, specification curve analysis, and vibration of effects. More broadly, the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) framework assesses how documented judgment calls across the data science life cycle affect conclusions, with predictability serving as a reality-check that a model captures signal. Each of these approaches results in a "multiverse" object. While the distribution of outcomes reflects the overall variability of conclusions, estimating the influence of each individual decision requires additional tools. A common heuristic is to train a model to predict the outcome from these decisions and treat its coefficients or feature importances as proxies for each decision's influence. Although this strategy may work in certain cases, it assumes the model is correctly specified and accurately predicts the outcome, which we show is not always the case. In this work, we introduce DECIDE, a model-free framework that quantifies each decision's importance from the actual outcomes across the plausible decision space, avoiding issues of predictability by design. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DECIDE by applying it to real-world multiverse analyses. We further provide what is, to our knowledge, the first formal definition of the multiverse.

Methodology.title: Metropolized backward sampling for conditional sequential Monte Carlo
Methodology.summary: Particle Gibbs samplers with backward sampling are widely used for sampling the smoothing distribution of state-space models, but, with few particles, the new trajectory often coincides with the current one at many time steps. A known but rarely used remedy replaces the random selection of the final particle by a Metropolis--Hastings move which avoids the current particle. We show that, with backward sampling, this remedy only helps at the last time steps, because its effect on the update rates decays geometrically with the distance to the final time. We propose instead Metropolized backward sampling, which makes such a move at every step of the backward pass, forcibly switching trajectories whenever possible. Additionally, we introduce a coupled version which prevents proposing the current trajectory, maximizing the chances of an actual switch versus the current trajectory and performing perfect sampling when the state-space model has no observations, a feature not shared by backward sampling. We prove that, at every time step, both methods dominate backward sampling as they update the state more often and have smaller lag-one autocorrelations than it does. Our methods are drop-in replacements for backward sampling, and can be used to improve any particle Gibbs sampler.
Methodology.comment: 12 pages + appendix. A Lean formalization was AI-generated after the draft of the paper was written as an experiment. I have subsequently edited the documentation of the formalization for better readability, and discussed the process, as well as difference between the AI-formalized and my original proofs in the appendix. https://adriencorenflos.github.io/formalization/metropolized-CSMC/

Methodology.title: Integrating multi-source local information for global undirected graph reconstruction via integer programming
Methodology.summary: Graphical models are widely used to represent conditional independence structures, but learning them is challenging when data are fragmented across sources that measure different subsets of variables and may not be directly shareable. We develop a general framework for reconstructing a shared global graph from heterogeneous, partially observed sources. Our framework permits both the observed variable sets and source-specific distributions to differ. Under a source-wise faithfulness condition, local conditional independence graphs correspond to latent projections of the shared global graph, which is identifiable up to the equivalence class induced by the observed variable sets. The framework integrates raw data, estimated source graphs, or a combination of both, accommodating settings with restricted access to individual-level data, such as privacy constraints. We develop mixed-integer optimization formulations and scalable approximate algorithms for several classes of graphical models. Unlike standard high-dimensional analyses, our guarantees are governed by new combinatorial notions of signal strength that capture how information propagates across partially observed sources. Extensive simulations further show that integration can substantially improve estimation of source-specific projected graphs relative to separate source methods. Real-data application illustrates the framework's use with partially-observed sources of fatty acid measurements.

Methodology.title: Reframing Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons as a Transportability Problem: An Estimand-Based Perspective and Implications for Health Technology Assessment
Methodology.summary: Population-adjusted indirect comparisons (PAICs) are widely used to synthesize evidence when randomized controlled trials enroll different patient populations and head-to-head comparisons are unavailable. Although PAICs adjust for observed population differences across trials, adjustment alone does not ensure transportability of estimated effects to decision-relevant populations for health technology assessment (HTA). We examine and formalize transportability in PAICs from an estimand-based perspective. We distinguish conditional and marginal treatment effect estimands and show how transportability depends on effect modification, collapsibility, and alignment between the scale of effect modification and the effect measure. Using illustrative examples, we demonstrate that even when effect modifiers are shared across treatments, marginal effects are generally population-dependent for commonly used non-collapsible measures, including hazard ratios and odds ratios. Conversely, collapsible and conditional effects defined on the linear predictor scale exhibit more favorable transportability properties. We further show that pairwise PAIC approaches typically identify effects defined in the comparator population and that applying these estimates to other populations entails an additional, often implicit, transport step requiring further assumptions. This has direct implications for HTA, where PAIC-derived effects are routinely applied within cost-effectiveness and decision models defined for different target populations. Our results clarify when applying PAIC-derived treatment effects to desired target populations is justified, when doing so requires additional assumptions, and when results should instead be interpreted as population-specific rather than decision-relevant, supporting more transparent and principled use of indirect evidence in HTA and related decision-making contexts.
Methodology.comment: 26 pages (excluding supplement and references), 7 figures, 1 table

Methodology.title: Optimal Experimental Design for the Polynomial Maximization Method: a Higher-Order Reserve Beyond Second-Order Design Theory
Methodology.summary: Optimal designs for regression with asymmetric errors build on the second-order least squares estimator (SLSE) of Wang and Leblanc (2008), whose gain over ordinary least squares (OLS) comes from the error skewness. With i.i.d. errors the optimally weighted SLSE solves the same estimating equation as the degree-two Polynomial Maximization Method (PMM), a family whose degree-$S$ location estimator has asymptotic variance $g_S\le1$ times that of the sample mean. We derive optimal designs for this family when the errors are independent with constant variance but have standardised cumulants of order three and higher that vary with the regressor (cumulant heteroscedasticity). For a known reduction field $g_S(x)$, the $g_S$-weighted information matrix $M_{g_S}$ obeys the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem. A constant field leaves the OLS-optimal design unchanged; a non-constant field can change it but need not. For symmetric errors with varying kurtosis, the PMM$_2$ and conditional-SLSE designs cannot depart from the OLS-optimal one, whereas a degree-three design can. A stratify-and-pool PMM$_S$ estimator attains $N\mathrm{Cov}(\hatθ)\toσ^2M_{g_S}^{-1}$ at every degree as all strata grow; its per-stratum reduction is below one only for symmetric errors with the symmetry imposed. For a quadratic model on $[0,1]$ with symmetric Beta errors of unit variance and dose-varying shape, the third-order design for the known field has $A$-efficiency $1.047$ relative to the OLS-optimal design, and $1.001$ under the $D$-criterion. A two-stage procedure that estimates the field from a one-third pilot builds designs of $A$-efficiency $1.014$-$1.020$ at $N=600$-$2400$; its realised mean-squared-error ratio against the OLS-optimal design ranges from $0.89$ (a loss) to $1.08$.
Methodology.comment: 41 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Companion to arXiv:2606.11421 (second-order least squares as the degree-two polynomial maximization method). v3: adds the cost of a small asymmetry and the limit of plug-in designs; corrects the two-stage limit; code supplement v1.0.2

Methodology.title: SPACR: Single-Pass Adaptive Training of Uncertainty-Aware Conformal Regressors
Methodology.summary: Conformal Prediction (CP) provides robust uncertainty guarantees for predictive models, but is typically applied post hoc, which misaligns model training with the conformal goal of producing efficient (i.e., narrow) intervals. We propose SPACR (Single-Pass Adaptive Conformal Regressor), a novel method for directly training uncertainty-aware regressors within a differentiable loss. SPACR jointly optimizes accuracy, efficiency, and validity without batch-splitting or a predefined confidence level during training. As a result, a single SPACR model yields valid prediction intervals at multiple confidence levels during inference, avoiding the costly retraining required by methods like Directly Optimized Inductive Conformal Regression (DOICR). Experiments on diverse tabular and image datasets show that SPACR consistently gives tighter intervals and better coverage-efficiency trade-offs compared to standard CP and DOICR, while significantly reducing computational costs relative to retraining-dependent baselines.

Methodology.title: Optimal approximation error approach in Bayesian inverse problems
Methodology.summary: In many inverse problems, evaluating the forward operator is computationally expensive, making it common practice to accelerate inference with a less costly approximate model. However, such approximations introduce unwanted bias and must be carefully accounted for to ensure the reliability of the solution. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in Bayesian inference, where accurate posterior characterisation typically requires a large number of forward model evaluations. In this paper, we focus on the approximation error model (AEM), which compensates for the modelling error by adjusting the likelihood density. More precisely, AEM incorporates the model error into the additive Gaussian noise distribution. A central challenge in this approach is how to choose the modified noise mean and covariance in a principled way. To address this, we propose a new framework, optimal approximation error (OAE) which determines the noise model by minimising the expected information loss, measured via the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the true and approximate posterior distributions. We show that the standard enhanced error approach (EEA) is recovered as the minimiser of the expected divergence between likelihoods rather than posteriors and develop OAE as a direct alternative targeting posterior accuracy. We establish bi-convexity of the OAE objective, introduce a regularised, provably convergent proximal alternating minimisation scheme, and derive closed-form expressions in the Gaussian linear setting. We further show that OAE estimates computed from empirical training data are statistically consistent. Numerical experiments on a linear CT problem and a nonlinear Darcy-flow problem show that OAE improves posterior accuracy relative to both the uncorrected and EEA-corrected likelihoods.

Methodology.title: Robust Global Testing for Mean Functions in Sparse and Dense Functional and Longitudinal Data
Methodology.summary: We develop a robust quadratic score test for a specified mean function in functional and longitudinal data. The construction combines a convex loss with subject-level scores while retaining dependence among repeated measurements. An explicit score-centering condition ensures that the target remains the population mean. We establish the null distribution and Sobolev separation rates under sparse and dense sampling, identifying a transition from a nonparametric testing rate to the root-n boundary. A Gaussian multiplier bootstrap remains valid across these regimes, including settings with non-Gaussian quadratic limits. For implementation, we use a finite spline approximation and estimate the curvature through symmetric score increments. Under the stated conditions, the feasible procedure preserves null calibration and attains a consistency separation rate matching the lower bound over model classes containing a Gaussian submodel. Simulations illustrate the performance of squared, Huber, and absolute losses under regular errors and contamination, and an analysis of longitudinal CD4 counts demonstrates the method.

Methodology.title: Combining Adaptive Seamless Phase II/III Designs and Group Sequential Analysis for Time-to-Event Endpoints in Oncology Trials
Methodology.summary: Seamless Phase II/III designs are a natural vehicle for the randomized dose optimization called for by the US Food and Drug Administration's Project Optimus initiative. Their extension to group sequential repeated testing of a time-to-event endpoint after end-of-Phase-II dose selection, however, remains largely unestablished. Existing proposals index the boundaries for the post-selection looks by the overall information fraction of the primary endpoint---the correct index for the log-rank statistics of an unadapted trial, but not for the combination statistics these designs actually test---and support family-wise error rate (FWER) control by simulation. We instead work from the joint distribution of the combination statistics themselves, calibrating group sequential boundaries separately for each hypothesis in the closure and applying closed testing at every look; a general lemma establishes that this controls the FWER in the strong sense, for any number of hypotheses and analysis times. Specifically, under patient-wise separation and an inverse-normal combination test, the interim and final statistics for an individual hypothesis are bivariate normal, with a correlation determined by how the events at each look divide between the pre- and post-selection cohorts rather than by the overall information fraction, so that their boundaries follow from standard group sequential software; the corresponding statistics for the intersection hypothesis, formed from a Hochberg-adjusted Stage-1 $p$-value, are not multivariate normal, and we obtain their boundaries by a dedicated numerical integration. Head-to-head against a recently proposed incremental-Dunnett procedure, the two were near-identical when the design projections were correct, but ours was more robust when the combination weights were based on a misprojected division of the Stage~1 events either side of the interim.

Methodology.title: A sensitivity analysis for the average derivative effect
Methodology.summary: In observational studies, exposures are often continuous rather than binary or discrete. At the same time, sensitivity analysis is an important tool that can help determine the robustness of a causal conclusion to a certain level of unmeasured confounding, which can never be ruled out in an observational study. Sensitivity analysis approaches for continuous exposures have now been proposed for several causal estimands. In this article, we focus on the average derivative effect (ADE). We obtain closed-form bounds for the ADE under a sensitivity model that constrains the odds ratio (at any two dose levels) between the latent and observed generalized propensity score. We propose flexible, efficient estimators for the bounds that are compatible with machine learning algorithms as well as point-wise and simultaneous (over the sensitivity parameter) confidence intervals. We examine the finite sample performance of the methods through simulations and illustrate the methods on a study assessing the effect of parental income on educational attainment and a study assessing the price elasticity of petrol.
Methodology.comment: Fix formatting issues; Some changes to exposition and references

Methodology.title: Graphical Model-based Inference on Persistent Homology
Methodology.summary: Persistent homology is a cornerstone of topological data analysis, offering a multiscale summary of topology with robustness to nuisance transformations, such as rotations and small deformations. Persistent homology has seen broad use across domains such as computer vision and neuroscience. Most statistical treatments, however, use homology primarily as a feature extractor, relying on statistical distance-based tests or simple time-to-event models for inferential tasks. While these approaches can detect global differences, they rarely localize the source of those differences. We address this gap by taking a graphical model-based approach: we associate each vertex with a population latent position in a conic space and model each bar's key events (birth and death times) using an exponential distribution, whose rate is a transformation of the latent positions according to an event occurring on the graph. The low-dimensional bars have simple graph-event representations, such as the formation of a minimum spanning tree or the triangulation of a loop, and thus enjoy tractable likelihoods. Taking a Bayesian approach, we infer latent positions and enable model extensions such as hierarchical models that allow borrowing strength across groups. Applications to a neuroimaging study of Alzheimer's disease demonstrate that our method localizes sources of difference and provides interpretable, model-based analyses of topological structure in complex data. The code is provided and maintained at https://github.com/zitian-wu/graphPH.

Methodology.title: Latent community paths in VAR-type models via dynamic directed spectral co-clustering
Methodology.summary: This paper proposes a dynamic network framework for uncovering latent community paths in high-dimensional VAR-type models. By embedding a degree-corrected stochastic co-blockmodel (ScBM) into the transition matrices of VAR-type systems, we separate sending and receiving roles at the node level and summarize complex directional dependence in an interpretable low-dimensional form. Our method integrates directed spectral co-clustering with eigenvector smoothing to track how directional groups split, merge, or persist over time. This framework accommodates both periodic VAR (PVAR) models for cyclical seasonal evolution and generalized VHAR models for structural transitions across ordered dependence horizons. We establish non-asymptotic misclassification bounds for both procedures and provide supporting evidence through Monte Carlo experiments. Applications to U.S. nonfarm payrolls distinguish a recurrent business-centered core from more mobile, seasonally sensitive sectors. In global stock volatilities, the results reveal a compact U.S.-centered long-horizon block, a Europe-heavy developed core, and a more dynamic short-horizon reallocation of peripheral and bridge markets.

Methodology.title: On the Spherical Dirichlet Distribution: Corrections and Results
Methodology.summary: This article revisits the spherical-Dirichlet distribution (SDD) introduced by Guardiola (2020) and clarifies the correction to its density presented in an earlier version of this preprint. The principal issue concerns Equation (3) of the original publication, which expresses the density in local Euclidean coordinates rather than with respect to spherical surface-area measure. We derive the corrected intrinsic density and revisit its moments, covariance matrix, mode, and limiting properties. We show that the two density representations describe the same probability distribution, preserving the moment formulas and likelihood-based parameter estimation. However, the mode and uniformity conditions depend on the reference measure and require corresponding clarification. Reported simulation and text mining estimates are revisited and updated. The resulting presentation reconciles the original construction with its intrinsic spherical properties.
Methodology.comment: 9 pages, 1 figure with four panels. Revised to clarify coordinate and spherical surface-area densities, mode and uniformity conditions, and parameter estimation; numerical summaries updated. Corrects and extends Guardiola, J. Stat. Distrib. App. 7, 6 (2020), https://doi.org/10.1186/s40488-020-00106-9

Methodology.title: Optimal Expert Annotation for Evaluating Sequential Decision Policies from Text Records
Methodology.summary: Offline reinforcement learning and off-policy evaluation evaluate dynamic decision rules based on historical data, without the ability to deploy online. In recent artificial intelligence (AI) applications, simple state and reward information is recorded as complex text or image, expert annotation may be available but at a higher cost. Recent AI and machine learning (ML) predictors can label data cheaply but with unknown bias. We show how a limited budget for ground-truth data-annotation can safely make use of plentiful ML predictions in a new estimator for doubly-robust off-policy evaluation with missing rewards. Our method directs where data should be collected by optimizing annotation probabilities for the best downstream estimation variance, which we implement in a feasible batch-adaptive approach. Our work is motivated by a collaboration with a homelessness services nonprofit that writes casenotes for individuals over time. Our method can be used to unlock trustworthy inference from casenote data and answer new inferential questions such as: how does expanding outreach effort over time affect progress towards a housing application and improvement in housing placement? In simulations and on two real datasets -- casenotes from the nonprofit and human-preference votes from LMArena -- we see reductions in RMSE of 37-65% for housing placement and 21-67% for progress towards a housing application at budgets of 50% of full annotation and above, and by 55-62% at every budget on LMArena under an equal-exposure policy.

Methodology.title: Joint Distributional Copula Regression for Insurance Claim Frequency and Severity via Boosting
Methodology.summary: In this paper, we introduce a model-based boosting approach for fitting structured additive distributional copula regression models for bivariate responses, with particular emphasis on jointly modeling insurance claim frequency and severity. The approach uses regression-type base learners, such as linear terms and splines with low degrees of freedom. It builds on generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS), which extend generalized additive models (GAMs) by allowing multiple distributional parameters, rather than only the conditional mean, to depend on covariates. The structured additive predictors make the model inherently interpretable, offering greater transparency and auditability than black-box approaches. These features are particularly relevant in regulated actuarial settings and applications requiring explainable artificial intelligence. By estimating the entire conditional joint distribution, the framework also enables insurance practitioners to examine conditional quantiles, tail behavior, and prediction intervals of risks. The copula component captures dependence between claim frequency and severity and allows practitioners to investigate how this dependence varies with policyholder characteristics, potentially improving predictive performance. Moreover, by incorporating modern machine-learning techniques, specifically boosting, the proposed model improves prediction accuracy while retaining interpretability. We assess the proposed framework using both simulated and real data. The results demonstrate its ability to recover the true covariate effects on the marginal distributional parameters and the dependence structure, select informative variables, and achieve predictive performance competitive with standard benchmark models. We also illustrate how to interpret the fitted model.

Methodology.title: Weighting Scheme and Construction in IPCW Survival Estimation
Methodology.summary:
Inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) is widely used to address dependent censoring in survival analysis. Beyond estimation of the censoring distribution, its implementation requires specifying how inverse probability weights are incorporated into survival estimators. IPCW does not uniquely determine this construction, and different choices can produce different finite-sample behavior even under the same censoring model.
  In this work, we examine a class of IPCW estimators for the survival function, distinguishing hazard-based from margin-based formulations and time-varying from fixed weighting schemes. We show how these choices affect structural validity, stability, and finite-sample performance. In particular, the weight-changing hazard (WCH) estimator applies time-varying censoring weights within a product-limit construction with risk-set normalization, ensuring monotonicity and boundedness when the weighted risk-set denominators are positive. Through simulation studies under varying levels of covariate-dependent and administrative censoring, we demonstrate that WCH achieves favorable bias--variance tradeoffs and improved finite-sample stability relative to the alternative IPCW constructions examined, particularly in settings with few observed events or heavy censoring. We further illustrate these differences using data from the Women's Interagency HIV Study (WIHS), in which alternative IPCW constructions produced meaningfully different survival curves.
  Overall, our findings emphasize that the effectiveness of IPCW depends on both the weighting scheme and the estimator formulation. Careful consideration of these choices is therefore important for reliable survival estimation under dependent censoring.

Methodology.title: Bias-Aware External-Model-Assisted Inference in High-Dimensional Regression
Methodology.summary: In high-dimensional semi-supervised linear regression, prediction-powered inference (PPI) corrects an external predictor with a rectifier estimated from the labeled data. In a linear model, however, this rectifier cancels the predictor: PPI and PPI++ reduce to ordinary least squares and can inflate variance when the predictor is close to the oracle. We propose the Debiased External-model-Assisted Lasso (DEAL), which routes the external estimator and the unlabeled covariates into the variance of a debiased estimator, with a bias-aware, cross-fitted shrinkage step that adapts across target-only, near-oracle, and biased-but-informative regimes. We prove coordinate-wise asymptotic normality with an adaptive variance, extend validity to the projection parameter under misspecification and nonlinear labelers, and show that, at a common unlabeled budget, DEAL intervals are shorter than those of debiased Lasso, PPI, and PPI++; a shift-aware variant preserves coverage under covariate shift. In simulations, DEAL intervals are 0.49-0.87 of the debiased-Lasso length, and across six real-data applications spanning astronomy, chemistry, proteomics, and oncology, the last using a large-language-model oracle, they tighten in every case, with median length ratios of 0.23-0.53.

Methodology.title: L-PASSO: Adaptive Log-penalized Variable Selector, with Sparse Selection and Robustness to the Pilot Estimator
Methodology.summary: We study L-PASSO, a penalized least-squares regression method based on the logarithmic penalty $λ\sum_j\log(1+|β_j|/τ)$, and its two-stage adaptive form, in which the scales $τ_j$ come from a pilot estimator. Although this concave penalty has been proposed previously, its variable-selection properties and sparsity relative to other popular penalties have not been fully characterized. We derive the exact orthogonal-design solution, and show that the single-stage estimator selects the true model under a weighted irrepresentable condition that holds for every design once $τ$ is small. We further establish that, under matched tuning, the two-stage estimator possesses the oracle property and has half the asymptotic bias of the adaptive LASSO. Our main theoretical contribution concerns the robustness of the two-stage procedure to the pilot estimator. We show that two-stage L-PASSO remains selection consistent even when the weights associated with relevant variables are as small as $\exp\{-o(1/ζ_n)\}$, whereas the adaptive LASSO fails to retain relevant variables whose pilot weights are sufficiently small relative to its tuning parameter $ζ_n$. We establish that both thresholds are sharp. In high-dimensional settings, we prove support recovery for a local minimizer without imposing any lower-bound condition on the weights of relevant variables, and provide conditions under which this local minimizer is also the unique global minimizer. We additionally establish the selection consistency of a BIC-based tuning-parameter selection procedure. Finally, simulations comparing L-PASSO with the LASSO, SCAD, MCP, SELO, uniLasso, and the adaptive LASSO show that L-PASSO most frequently recovers the true support. Two real-data examples further illustrate the method.

Graphics.title: MeshSuite: A Unified Benchmark for Triangle- and Mesh-Based Neural Rendering
Graphics.summary: Triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering seeks to bridge neural representations and graphics engines through triangle primitives compatible with standard rasterization. Yet existing methods were developed and evaluated under inconsistent settings, with few direct comparisons and little evaluation in graphics engines. We introduce MeshSuite, the first benchmark for systematic evaluation of engine deployment and Non-Engine Render in triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering. MeshSuite evaluates two deployment settings: Standard Deployment, using an opaque mesh pipeline with vertex colors and hardware Z-buffering; and Dedicated Deployment, using method-specific engine implementations to preserve appearance and compositing features. For mesh splatting, we also audit exported surfaces for topological and geometric integrity as downstream graphics assets. Our results show that engine deployment reduces image quality in both settings; among evaluated methods, MeshSplatting degrades least under Standard Deployment. Dedicated Deployment preserves most fidelity at roughly 5-33x the runtime of Standard Deployment across two deployment datasets. For mesh splatting, explicit connectivity and shared indexing remain limited: shared vertex indexing alone guarantees neither manifoldness nor global connectivity. These findings show that rasterizability is only part of graphics readiness and underscore the need to assess engine deployment. Project page: https://x-up-lab.github.io/research/meshsuite.

Graphics.title: Evaluation of Gauss-Legendre curves
Graphics.summary: We present new representations of Gauss--Legendre polynomials and their derivatives in the shifted power basis and in bases related to symmetric orthogonal Jacobi polynomials. Using these representations and certain recurrence relations, we propose $O(n^2+dn)$ methods for evaluating a Gauss--Legendre curve of degree $n$ in $\mathbb E^d$. We also propose algorithms for multipoint evaluation with computational complexity $O(Mdn+dn^2)$, where $M$ is the number of evaluation points. Numerical tests show that the approach using the shifted power basis is very fast, but it works well only for small $n$ (approximately up to 20), whereas the method employing Jacobi polynomials gives good numerical results even for large $n$ (around 100).

Graphics.title: Fast subdivision of Bézier curves
Graphics.summary:
It is well-known that a $d$-dimensional polynomial Bézier curve of degree $n$ can be subdivided into two segments using the famous de Casteljau algorithm in $O(dn^2)$ time. We show that it is possible to do this in $O(dn\log{n})$ time using the fast Fourier transform and its inverse. The direct application of the method is numerically unstable for larger values of $n$. Therefore, we also introduce a modified version based on parameter scaling, which retains the same asymptotic computational complexity. This scaling approach can improve numerical accuracy in some cases (for $n\lesssim 50$), as demonstrated by our experiments. Moreover, the new method has a nice property: if a Bézier curve is extended by an additional control point, the subdivision can be updated in $O(d)$ time. The method can be adapted to subdivide rational Bézier curves and rectangular Bézier surfaces, as well as to compute the derivatives of Bézier curves.
  Although motivated by applications in CAGD, the proposed methods may also be useful in other areas involving polynomial reparameterization.

Graphics.title: Self-Consistency Geometry Injection for Multi-view Consistent Image Generation
Graphics.summary: Recent diffusion models have achieved impressive progress in single image to multi-view generation by synthesizing consistent novel views efficiently. Existing methods usually explicitly or implicitly couple geometry inference and texture synthesis, making generation vulnerable to inaccurate geometry prediction. Although several geometry-guided methods have explored decoupling, they usually treat predicted geometry as a fixed condition and do not explicitly model whether the geometry is reliable. We therefore propose Reliability-Guided Multi-View Generation (RGMV), which comprises a parameter-free Self-Consistency Geometry Gate (SCG) and a Reliability-aware Geometry Injection (RGI) module. Specifically, a geometry proposal generator produces multiple geometry predictions for the same reference image and target viewpoints under different stochastic sampling configurations. SCG measures their spatial agreement to derive a reliability map, which RGI uses to modulate the injection strength of geometry-conditioned residuals in the RGB synthesis model. Moreover, RGMV can adapt to different geometry proposal generators. As a result, RGMV preserves stronger geometric guidance in stable regions while attenuating unreliable geometry cues before they propagate into multi-view RGB generation. Extensive experiments show that reliability-aware geometry injection improves the geometric quality of multi-view generation. Code: https://github.com/WISLab-GDUT/RGMV.

Graphics.title: X2HDR: HDR Image Generation in a Perceptually Uniform Space
Graphics.summary: High-dynamic-range (HDR) formats and displays are becoming increasingly prevalent, yet state-of-the-art image generators (e.g., Stable Diffusion and FLUX) typically remain limited to low-dynamic-range (LDR) output due to the lack of large-scale HDR training data. In this work, we show that existing pretrained diffusion models can be easily adapted to HDR generation without retraining from scratch. A key challenge is that HDR images are natively represented in linear RGB, whose intensity and color statistics differ substantially from those of sRGB-encoded LDR images. This gap, however, can be effectively bridged by converting HDR inputs into perceptually uniform encodings (e.g., using PU21 or PQ). Empirically, we find that LDR-pretrained variational autoencoders (VAEs) reconstruct PU21-encoded HDR inputs with fidelity comparable to LDR data, whereas linear RGB inputs cause severe degradations. Motivated by this finding, we describe an efficient adaptation strategy that freezes the VAE and finetunes only the denoiser via low-rank adaptation in a perceptually uniform space. This results in a unified computational method that supports both text-to-HDR synthesis and single-image RAW-to-HDR reconstruction. Experiments demonstrate that our perceptually encoded adaptation consistently improves perceptual fidelity, text-image alignment, and effective dynamic range, relative to previous techniques.

Graphics.title: Neural Explicit Shape Representation
Graphics.summary: Existing neural 3D representations separately address continuous surface modeling, efficient image synthesis, or object-specific compression. They do not jointly provide the explicit surface queries required by ray tracing and a structured output space that can be predicted across objects. We introduce NeuOctree, a neural explicit representation that directly predicts whether and where a ray intersects a surface, together with its normal and albedo. NeuOctree stores shared features at the corners of sparse octree voxels and interpolates them into a continuous local field. A lightweight decoder with recurrent intersection-guided sampling refines each query near the predicted surface, enabling direct surface rendering without mesh extraction or texture baking and accommodating open, non-watertight geometry. The same octree structure supports both compact per-object optimization and a shared octree CNN that constructs renderable assets from colored point clouds without per-object fitting. Across seven meshes and four storage budgets, NeuOctree achieves the lowest positional error in 24 of 28 comparisons while retaining competitive normal accuracy, and substantially improves joint geometry--appearance reconstruction over N-BVH and VQAD. The feedforward model constructs a representation in 0.05 seconds and transfers from Objaverse to ShapeNet without retraining. We further demonstrate ray-traced rendering and image-conditioned generation, showing that NeuOctree provides a common output space for neural inference and direct surface rendering. Code is available at https://github.com/octree-nn/neural-octree.

Graphics.title: Turbo4DGen: Ultra-Fast Acceleration for 4D Generation
Graphics.summary: 4D generation, or dynamic 3D content generation, integrates spatial, temporal, and view dimensions to model realistic dynamic scenes, playing a foundational role in advancing world models and physical AI. However, maintaining long-chain consistency across both frames and viewpoints through the unique spatio-camera-motion (SCM) attention mechanism introduces substantial computational and memory overhead, often leading to out-of-memory (OOM) failures and prohibitive generation times. To address these challenges, we propose Turbo4DGen, an ultra-fast acceleration framework for diffusion-based multi-view 4D content generation. Turbo4DGen introduces a spatiotemporal cache mechanism that persistently reuses intermediate attention across denoising steps, combined with dynamically semantic-aware attention pruning and an adaptive SCM chain bypass scheduler, to drastically reduce redundant SCM attention computation. Our experimental results show that Turbo4DGen achieves an average 9.7$\times$ speedup without quality degradation on the ObjaverseDy and Consistent4D datasets. To the best of our knowledge, Turbo4DGen is the first dedicated acceleration framework for 4D generation.

Graphics.title: 3DCodeEdit: Benchmarking Instruction-Guided 3D Program Editing
Graphics.summary: Language models increasingly create 3D content through code, with practical workflows often relying on editing existing programs rather than regenerating them, for speed and precise control. Such edits require understanding what a program builds and foreseeing how a change reshapes it, yet prior benchmarks mostly evaluate generation or simple edits against a reference. In this paper, we introduce 3DCodeEdit, a benchmark of 2,592 instruction-guided editing tasks over 108 Blender programs that construct objects entirely in code. Its edits range from parameter to structural changes, style redesign, and scene composition, and are judged from renders against human-reviewed checklists. Across 17 models, the average success rate is only 37%, and even the strongest models complete fewer than 60% of structural and style edits. As models become more capable, their failures shift to geometric foresight, where the code runs but builds the wrong shape. We therefore study whether multi-turn feedback can compensate for this missing foresight. Feedback from a separate reviewer model that describes how the renders differ from the request helps most, more than maximum reasoning effort or an agent harness, and can let a 27B model surpass the single-shot rate of a 2.8T-parameter model.

Graphics.title: HyperIntent: Tracking Intent Shifts for Efficient Reasoning on Dynamic Textual Graphs
Graphics.summary: Dynamic web interactions continuously evolve as new edges arrive, offering large language models (LLMs) great potential for reasoning over edge-level temporal semantics. However, continuously arriving edges are often repetitive, obscuring the key structures that truly reflect temporal changes and limiting the efficiency of LLMs. A key insight is that beneath the dense stream of edge arrivals lies a sparse evolution of temporal intent, enabling LLMs to be responsively triggered only when such intent shifts, while otherwise inheriting the previous state. To this end, we propose a hypergraph-based framework named HyperIntent, which enhances dynamic graph reasoning by parsing differentiated intents, quantifying their temporal discrepancies, and performing shift-triggered semantic updating. Experimental results on destination node retrieval and future link prediction demonstrate that HyperIntent consistently achieves the best overall performance, with average relative Hits@1 gains of 34.0% and 25.4% over vanilla TGAT and DyGFormer, respectively. Meanwhile, HyperIntent reduces LLM token consumption by 54.4%-95.9% across six datasets while achieving leading predictive performance. In-depth studies further confirm the necessity of shift triggering for identifying structural and semantic temporal changes. The code will be made publicly available upon completion of the review process.
